**E. Second and fourth**

The four Vaganova arabesques are distinguished by épaulement / port de bras with the leg en arabesque derrière, not by the leg line alone.

* Arabesque I – ouvert / en face. The arms are kept essentially in a wide second/open line, more or less frontal and symmetrical about the torso. There is no clear single arm carried en avant on the supporting side; any forward bias is on the working-leg side.

* Arabesque III – effacée / open. The arms are brought together in front of the body in the Vaganova 3rd / effacée port de bras. The body is opened effacée to the working leg and the leading/forward carriage is on the working / lifted side. The forward arm is therefore on the same side as the lifted leg and the classic long front-back opposition is lost or reversed. I and III are the ouvert/effacée pair.

The croisée / opposition arabesques are II and IV.

* Arabesque II – croisée / classic opposition. Body in profile on the supporting leg, working leg en arabesque behind. Port de bras is a long front-back line: the arm belonging to the supporting side is brought forward at shoulder height in front of the torso and the arm belonging to the working side is taken back in line with the leg. The forward arm is on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg.

* Arabesque IV – inclined croisée / cambré opposition. The same opposition principle as II is retained with a deeper cambré/inclination of the torso and a lower carriage of the back arm. The supporting-side arm remains carried forward in front of the torso and the working-side arm remains carried back in line with the leg. The forward arm is again the supporting-side arm, i.e. on the opposite side of the body to the lifted working leg, the II/IV pair being the Vaganova croisée arabesques.

It is therefore the croisée arabesques II and IV that give the familiar Vaganova front-arm-opposite / back-arm-same contraposition with an arm extended in front on the opposite side to the lifted leg. I and III are the ouvert/effacée forms where that clear opposite-side forward projection is lost or reversed.
public_text.13:
B. Second and third

I think the confusion is coming from conflating croisée épaulement with the specific port de bras requirement of “arm extended in front on the opposite side to the lifted leg”.

Arabesque II is the undisputed classic. Body en profil on the supporting leg, working leg en arabesque derrière, arms in a long front-back line. The supporting-side arm is carried forward at shoulder height in front of the torso and the working-side arm is taken back in line with the leg. That forward arm is on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg.

Arabesque III keeps that same opposition logic. It is taught as the lower / more cambré, softer development of II. The torso opens a little more and the carriage is lower, the port de bras is more rounded and the arms are a little closer to the body, but the arm logic is preserved: the arm on the side of the standing leg is still the one projected forward in front of the torso and the arm on the side of the working leg is still carried back/up along the line of the leg. The forward arm remains the supporting-side arm, i.e. on the opposite side to the lifted leg. That is why II and III are routinely paired in class as the opposition arabesques, II being the high classical opposition and III being the same opposition with a deeper cambré and a lower arm placement.

Arabesque I is ouvert/effacée with the arms essentially in a wide second/open attitude, no clear forward cross on the supporting side.

Arabesque IV is the one that breaks the clear front-opposite pattern in Vaganova practice. In the syllabus IV is the closed / inclined / effacée variant. The torso is more inclined and the arms move toward a more rounded second/4th port de bras, brought more together in front of the body. The clear supporting-side forward projection of II and III is lost; the line is more to the side and rounded, the forward placement is no longer reliably on the supporting side opposite the lifted leg in the way it is in II and III. 

So the two positions where you actually get a distinct arm extended in front on the opposite side to the lifted leg are II and III. II is the classic croisée opposition, III is the lower cambré continuation of that same opposition.

The forward arm is therefore on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg.
* Arabesque IV – croisée inclinée / cambré. The same opposition principle is retained with a deeper cambré / inclination of the torso and a lower carriage of the back arm. The supporting-side arm remains carried forward in front of the torso and the working-side arm remains carried back in line with the leg. The forward arm is again the supporting-side arm, i.e. on the opposite side of the body to the lifted working leg.

It is the two croisée arabesques, II and IV, that give the characteristic Vaganova front-arm-opposite / back-arm-same contraposition with a distinct arm extended in front on the supporting / opposite side to the lifted leg. I and III are the ouvert / effacée forms in which that clear opposite-side forward projection is lost or reversed.

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The deliberation has moved from a Round 0 plurality for B. Second and third toward a Round 2 majority for E. Second and fourth, with the dispute now essentially II/IV croisée vs II/III opposition.

Current public split in Round 2:
E. Second and fourth – Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7. Argument: II and IV are the Vaganova croisée/opposition arabesques. Body en profil on supporting leg, working leg derrière, port de bras in a long front-back line: supporting-side arm carried forward at shoulder height in front of torso, working-side arm carried back in line with leg. Forward arm is therefore on the opposite side to lifted leg. IV is the inclined/cambré variant of II, same opposition principle retained with deeper épaulement/inclination, lower carriage of back arm. I is ouvert/en face/effacée with arms essentially in wide second/open line, no clear forward cross on supporting side; III is effacée/open with arms brought together in front in port de bras III, forward/leading arm on working/lifted side, torso opened effacée to leg. Hence I and III are the ouvert/effacée pair, forward arm same side as lifted leg or lost.

B. Second and third – Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9. Argument: II is classic croisée opposition with forward arm opposite lifted leg. III keeps the same opposition logic, taught as lower/more cambré/softened development of II: torso opens more, port de bras lower/rounded, but arm logic preserved – arm on standing/supporting side still projected forward in front of torso, arm on working side carried back/up. Forward arm remains supporting-side/opposite. I is ouvert/en face with arms in low second, no clear forward opposition. IV is the closed/inclined/effacée variant where the clear supporting-side forward projection is lost, arms move toward rounded second/4th port de bras, more to side and in front, forward placement no longer reliably opposite.

Key preserved definitional feature: supporting-side arm forward = forward arm opposite lifted leg, working-side arm back. Disagreement is mapping of III and IV.

III disputed: E camp describes III as effacée with port de bras III, arms in front, forward emphasis on working-leg side, same-side forward. B camp describes III as softer/lower II retaining opposite-side forward arm.

IV disputed: E camp describes IV as croisée inclined cambré, opposition retained – forward arm remains supporting-side/opposite. B camp describes IV as closed/rounded/effacée with arm placement shifted toward working-leg side, clear forward-opposite projection lost.

Changes in belief observed: several colleagues moved from A/C/B to E in Round 2, strengthening croisée II/IV pairing. Earlier minority A First and second and C First and third positions have largely disappeared.

Unresolved: canonical Vaganova numbering for the opposite-side forward arm. Need authoritative textual source to settle whether Vaganova III retains II opposition with lower carriage or is the effacée same-side-forward arabesque, and whether IV is the inclined croisée opposition or a closed effacée variant. Terminology confusion between ouvert/effacée vs croisée and port de bras I-III persists.

Current leaning in my synthesis remains with the majority croisée description: II and IV are the two arabesques with a distinct arm extended in front on the supporting/opposite side to the lifted leg, with I and III as the ouvert/effacée forms. This matches E. Second and fourth.

10.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The core dispute remains the mapping of Vaganova’s four arabesques to the criterion “arm extended in front on the side opposite the lifted leg”.

Consensus points:
* Arabesque II is undisputed classic croisée/opposition. Body en profil on supporting leg, working leg derrière, port de bras long front-back: supporting-side arm forward in front of torso, working-side arm back in line with leg. Forward arm is opposite lifted leg.
* Arabesque I is ouvert/en face/effacée. Arms essentially wide second/open, essentially symmetrical/frontal, no clear single forward arm on supporting side; any forward bias is on working-leg side.

Division:
* Majority E camp in round 2: 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7. Argument: croisée pair is II and IV. IV = croisée inclinée/cambré variant of II. Torso more inclined/deeper cambré than II but arm logic retained: forward arm remains supporting-side arm carried in front, back arm working-side. Forward arm again opposite lifted leg. III is effacée/open: arms brought together in front in Vaganova effacée/3rd port de bras, forward/leading arm on working/lifted side, i.e. forward arm same side as lifted leg, opposition reversed/lost. I and III are ouvert/effacée pair.
* Minority B camp in round 2: 13,14,2,5,8,9. Argument: II is classic opposition. III keeps same opposition logic, just lower/softened/cambré development of II. Supporting-side arm still projected forward in front of torso, working-side arm back/up along leg. Forward arm remains opposite lifted leg. IV is the problem: taught as closed/inclined/effacée variant with arms moved toward rounded second/4th port de bras, more to side/in front of body, clear supporting-side forward projection lost/softened. Therefore the two positions with a distinct arm extended in front on the opposite side are II and III.

Notable shifts: Colleague 12 moved from A. First and second in round 0 to E. Second and fourth in round 2. Colleague 3 moved from C. First and third in round 0 to E. Second and fourth in round 2.

Unresolved points that remain critical:
* Exact Vaganova port de bras of Arabesque III: effacée with forward arm on working-leg side, or lower softened version of II with forward arm still on supporting side?
* Exact port de bras of Arabesque IV: inclined croisée retaining II opposition with forward arm still supporting side, or closed/effacée with rounded 4th carriage where clear supporting-side forward projection is lost?
* Whether “arm extended in front” is interpreted strictly as a crisp shoulder-height forward extension vs a softer inclined projection.

Current best belief unchanged from previous round: under standard Vaganova croisée/effacée reading, the two arabesques with the arm extended in front on the opposite side to the lifted leg are the croisée pair II and IV, i.e. E. Second and fourth. Main risk remains school-specific naming variation for III vs IV sustaining the B. Second and third view. Need definitive Vaganova source to lock port de bras III vs IV.

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The anchor remains stable: Arabesque II is universally identified as the classic Vaganova croisée/opposition arabesque with the forward/leading arm on the supporting side, i.e. opposite the lifted leg behind, back arm on the working-leg side.

The dispute is now tightly concentrated on the partner to II, II+III vs II+IV.

E. Second and fourth camp, plurality in round 2 ~12 of 18:
* Arabesque I = ouvert/en face/effacée, arms in wide second/open, essentially symmetrical/frontal, no clear forward cross on supporting side; any forward bias is on working-leg side.
* Arabesque III = effacée/open, arms brought together in front in Vaganova 3rd/effacée port de bras, forward/leading arm is on the working/lifted side, i.e. forward prominence is on same side as lifted leg, torso opened effacée to leg. I and III are the ouvert/effacée pair.
* Arabesque II = croisée/opposition, forward arm supporting-side opposite lifted leg.
* Arabesque IV = croisée inclinée/cambré, same opposition principle as II retained with deeper cambré/inclination; forward arm remains supporting-side in front of torso, back arm on working-leg side. II/IV are the Vaganova croisée pair. The difference between II and IV is degree of épaulement/inclination, not reversal of opposition.

B. Second and third camp, minority ~6 of 18:
* Arabesque I = ouvert/en face, arms in low second/open, no clear forward opposition.
* Arabesque IV = closed/rounded second/4th/effacée inclined variant; torso more cambré, arms move toward rounded second/fourth, forward projection is softened/lost, no longer a clear arm extended in front on supporting side opposite leg.
* Arabesque II = classic opposition, forward arm opposite lifted leg.
* Arabesque III = lower/softened cambré development of II, torso more opened/lower/cambré but arm logic preserved: supporting-side arm still forward in front of torso, working-side arm back; forward arm remains opposite lifted leg. II and III are routinely taught as the opposition pair.

Unresolved points persisting:
* Whether Arabesque III retains II opposition with supporting-side forward arm, or switches to effacée with forward arm on working-leg side.
* Whether Arabesque IV is a croisée opposition like II with a clear forward arm opposite leg, or a closed/effacée inclined variant where the clear forward extension is lost/rounded.
* The precise meaning of “arm extended in front” – textbook croisée label vs studio practice of a distinct forward extension at shoulder height.
* Nomenclature drift between ouvert/effacée vs croisée labeling across teachers/sources.

Current belief state: II is secure. The weight of public argument in round 2 remains with E. Second and fourth, with a coherent, repeated croisée II/IV reading and I/III ouvert/effacée reading. The B minority raises a credible practical point about the clarity of forward extension in IV and preservation of opposition in III. I am leaning toward E. Second and fourth as the most coherent Vaganova croisée pair, while retaining uncertainty about the exact port de bras definition of III and the exact studio treatment of IV’s forward extension.

12.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The core undisputed premise remains that Arabesque II is the classic Vaganova croisée opposition/croisée arabesque: body in profile on the supporting leg, working leg en arabesque behind, supporting-side arm brought forward at shoulder height and working-side arm taken back, so the forward arm is on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg.

The dispute is which other arabesque shares that forward-opposite arm line.

Round 2 public set shows a clear shift toward E. Second and fourth. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7 now argue E. Their claim:
* I = ouvert/effacée/en face, arms wide second/open, essentially symmetrical/frontal, no clear forward cross on supporting side.
* III = effacée/open, arms kept together in front in Vaganova port de bras III. Forward/leading arm is on the working/lifted side, i.e. forward arm same side as lifted leg, torso opened effacée to that leg. I and III are the ouvert/effacée pair.
* II = croisée opposition as above.
* IV = inclined croisée / cambré variant of II, same opposition logic retained: forward arm supporting side, back arm working side, forward arm opposite lifted leg; difference is deeper épaulement/inclination and lower carriage.

Minority B. Second and third maintained by Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9. Their claim:
* II = classic croisée opposition as above.
* III = lower/softened/open version of II, torso more opened/cambré, carriage lower/rounded, but arm logic preserved: supporting-side arm still projected forward in front of torso and working-side arm still back/up along line of leg, so forward arm remains opposite lifted leg. II and III are routinely taught as a paired opposition family, III being the cambré/softened II.
* I = ouvert with arms in wide second, no clear forward opposition.
* IV = closed/effacée/rounded, arms brought more together/in front, clear front-back opposition lost; forward projection no longer reliably on supporting side.

Distribution now ~ E 12 vs B 6, with earlier A first+second and C first+third voters having moved to E. Colleague 12,4 moved from A first+second to E; Colleague 17,18,3 moved from C first+third to E.

Noticing errors/confusion: several posts conflate port de bras numbering with arabesque numbering; some earlier inversions of I/II labels. The phrase “arm extended in front” is interpreted differently: E treats it as a clear front-back ligne with one arm distinctly in front on supporting side; B treats any forward carriage of supporting-side arm, even low/rounded, as qualifying.

My current best belief remains E. Second and fourth are the Vaganova croisée arabesques with the dancer’s arm extended in front on the opposite side to the lifted leg. I and III are the ouvert/effacée pair where that clear opposite-side forward projection is absent or reversed. Unresolved is whether Vaganova studio practice routinely teaches III with a retained opposite-side forward arm in the lower carriage, which sustains the B second+third claim. Need a definitive source on Vaganova’s official arabesque IV port de bras description and the exact arm height/shaping in III vs IV to close the III vs IV ambiguity.

7.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is which Vaganova arabesques have the supporting-side arm carried extended in front, i.e. on the opposite side to the lifted/working leg behind.

Core agreement:
* Arabesque II is undisputed classic croisée/contraposed opposition: body in profile on supporting leg, working leg en arabesque derrière, supporting-side arm brought forward at shoulder height in front of torso, working-side arm taken back in line with leg. Forward arm is opposite the lifted leg.
* Arabesque I is ouvert/en face/effacée: arms essentially in wide second/open, frontal/symmetrical, no clear single forward cross on supporting side; any forward bias is on working-leg side.

Split is I/III vs IV, and III vs IV.

E camp – II and IV are the croisée pair, I and III are ouvert/effacée/open.
* Arabesque III = effacée/open: arms brought together in front in Vaganova 3rd/effacée port de bras. Forward/leading arm is on the working/lifted side, i.e. forward carriage is on same side as lifted leg; classic front-back opposition is lost/reversed.
* Arabesque IV = croisée inclinée/cambré variant of II. Same arm logic as II: forward arm remains supporting-side, back arm working-side. Difference is deeper cambré/inclination and lower carriage, not reversal of opposition.
Therefore forward-arm-opposite-leg arabesques are II and IV. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7 reiterate this in round 2, stressing I & III as ouvert/effacée and II & IV as croisée.

B camp – II and III are the opposition pair, I and IV break the pattern.
* Arabesque III keeps II opposition logic, just lower/softened/cambré. Supporting-side arm is still projected forward in front of torso, working-side arm back/up. Forward arm remains opposite lifted leg; teachers routinely pair II+III as opposition arabesques.
* Arabesque IV is closed/inclined/effacée with port de bras IV: arms move toward rounded second/fourth, brought closer to body and more to side, clear supporting-side forward extension at shoulder height is lost/ softened. In studio practice forward projection is no longer reliably on opposite side.
Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9 argue this in round 2, emphasizing the wording “arm extended in front” as stricter than generic opposition.

Remaining uncertainty:
* Numbering/convention variability across studios.
* Precise description of Arabesque III arm placement: E camp says forward arm shifts to working-leg side in effacée 3rd port de bras; B camp says forward arm stays supporting-side but lower/rounded.

reflection_text.1:
The deliberation has moved from a Round 0 plurality for B. Second and third toward a Round 2 majority for E. Second and fourth, with the dispute now essentially II/IV croisée vs II/III opposition.

Current public split in Round 2:
E. Second and fourth – Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7. Argument: II and IV are the Vaganova croisée/opposition arabesques. Body en profil on supporting leg, working leg derrière, port de bras in a long front-back line: supporting-side arm carried forward at shoulder height in front of torso, working-side arm carried back in line with leg. Forward arm is therefore on the opposite side to lifted leg. IV is the inclined/cambré variant of II, same opposition principle retained with deeper épaulement/inclination, lower carriage of back arm. I is ouvert/en face/effacée with arms essentially in wide second/open line, no clear forward cross on supporting side; III is effacée/open with arms brought together in front in port de bras III, forward/leading arm on working/lifted side, torso opened effacée to leg. Hence I and III are the ouvert/effacée pair, forward arm same side as lifted leg or lost.

B. Second and third – Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9. Argument: II is classic croisée opposition with forward arm opposite lifted leg. III keeps the same opposition logic, taught as lower/more cambré/softened development of II: torso opens more, port de bras lower/rounded, but arm logic preserved – arm on standing/supporting side still projected forward in front of torso, arm on working side carried back/up. Forward arm remains supporting-side/opposite. I is ouvert/en face with arms in low second, no clear forward opposition. IV is the closed/inclined/effacée variant where the clear supporting-side forward projection is lost, arms move toward rounded second/4th port de bras, more to side and in front, forward placement no longer reliably opposite.

Key preserved definitional feature: supporting-side arm forward = forward arm opposite lifted leg, working-side arm back. Disagreement is mapping of III and IV.

III disputed: E camp describes III as effacée with port de bras III, arms in front, forward emphasis on working-leg side, same-side forward. B camp describes III as softer/lower II retaining opposite-side forward arm.

IV disputed: E camp describes IV as croisée inclined cambré, opposition retained – forward arm remains supporting-side/opposite. B camp describes IV as closed/rounded/effacée with arm placement shifted toward working-leg side, clear forward-opposite projection lost.

Changes in belief observed: several colleagues moved from A/C/B to E in Round 2, strengthening croisée II/IV pairing. Earlier minority A First and second and C First and third positions have largely disappeared.

Unresolved: canonical Vaganova numbering for the opposite-side forward arm. Need authoritative textual source to settle whether Vaganova III retains II opposition with lower carriage or is the effacée same-side-forward arabesque, and whether IV is the inclined croisée opposition or a closed effacée variant. Terminology confusion between ouvert/effacée vs croisée and port de bras I-III persists.

Current leaning in my synthesis remains with the majority croisée description: II and IV are the two arabesques with a distinct arm extended in front on the supporting/opposite side to the lifted leg, with I and III as the ouvert/effacée forms. This matches E. Second and fourth.
reflection_text.10:
The core dispute remains the mapping of Vaganova’s four arabesques to the criterion “arm extended in front on the side opposite the lifted leg”.

Consensus points:
* Arabesque II is undisputed classic croisée/opposition. Body en profil on supporting leg, working leg derrière, port de bras long front-back: supporting-side arm forward in front of torso, working-side arm back in line with leg. Forward arm is opposite lifted leg.
* Arabesque I is ouvert/en face/effacée. Arms essentially wide second/open, essentially symmetrical/frontal, no clear single forward arm on supporting side; any forward bias is on working-leg side.

Division:
* Majority E camp in round 2: 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7. Argument: croisée pair is II and IV. IV = croisée inclinée/cambré variant of II. Torso more inclined/deeper cambré than II but arm logic retained: forward arm remains supporting-side arm carried in front, back arm working-side. Forward arm again opposite lifted leg. III is effacée/open: arms brought together in front in Vaganova effacée/3rd port de bras, forward/leading arm on working/lifted side, i.e. forward arm same side as lifted leg, opposition reversed/lost. I and III are ouvert/effacée pair.
* Minority B camp in round 2: 13,14,2,5,8,9. Argument: II is classic opposition. III keeps same opposition logic, just lower/softened/cambré development of II. Supporting-side arm still projected forward in front of torso, working-side arm back/up along leg. Forward arm remains opposite lifted leg. IV is the problem: taught as closed/inclined/effacée variant with arms moved toward rounded second/4th port de bras, more to side/in front of body, clear supporting-side forward projection lost/softened. Therefore the two positions with a distinct arm extended in front on the opposite side are II and III.

Notable shifts: Colleague 12 moved from A. First and second in round 0 to E. Second and fourth in round 2. Colleague 3 moved from C. First and third in round 0 to E. Second and fourth in round 2.

Unresolved points that remain critical:
* Exact Vaganova port de bras of Arabesque III: effacée with forward arm on working-leg side, or lower softened version of II with forward arm still on supporting side?
* Exact port de bras of Arabesque IV: inclined croisée retaining II opposition with forward arm still supporting side, or closed/effacée with rounded 4th carriage where clear supporting-side forward projection is lost?
* Whether “arm extended in front” is interpreted strictly as a crisp shoulder-height forward extension vs a softer inclined projection.

Current best belief unchanged from previous round: under standard Vaganova croisée/effacée reading, the two arabesques with the arm extended in front on the opposite side to the lifted leg are the croisée pair II and IV, i.e. E. Second and fourth. Main risk remains school-specific naming variation for III vs IV sustaining the B. Second and third view. Need definitive Vaganova source to lock port de bras III vs IV.
reflection_text.4:
The anchor remains stable: Arabesque II is universally identified as the classic Vaganova croisée/opposition arabesque with the forward/leading arm on the supporting side, i.e. opposite the lifted leg behind, back arm on the working-leg side.

The dispute is now tightly concentrated on the partner to II, II+III vs II+IV.

E. Second and fourth camp, plurality in round 2 ~12 of 18:
* Arabesque I = ouvert/en face/effacée, arms in wide second/open, essentially symmetrical/frontal, no clear forward cross on supporting side; any forward bias is on working-leg side.
* Arabesque III = effacée/open, arms brought together in front in Vaganova 3rd/effacée port de bras, forward/leading arm is on the working/lifted side, i.e. forward prominence is on same side as lifted leg, torso opened effacée to leg. I and III are the ouvert/effacée pair.
* Arabesque II = croisée/opposition, forward arm supporting-side opposite lifted leg.
* Arabesque IV = croisée inclinée/cambré, same opposition principle as II retained with deeper cambré/inclination; forward arm remains supporting-side in front of torso, back arm on working-leg side. II/IV are the Vaganova croisée pair. The difference between II and IV is degree of épaulement/inclination, not reversal of opposition.

B. Second and third camp, minority ~6 of 18:
* Arabesque I = ouvert/en face, arms in low second/open, no clear forward opposition.
* Arabesque IV = closed/rounded second/4th/effacée inclined variant; torso more cambré, arms move toward rounded second/fourth, forward projection is softened/lost, no longer a clear arm extended in front on supporting side opposite leg.
* Arabesque II = classic opposition, forward arm opposite lifted leg.
* Arabesque III = lower/softened cambré development of II, torso more opened/lower/cambré but arm logic preserved: supporting-side arm still forward in front of torso, working-side arm back; forward arm remains opposite lifted leg. II and III are routinely taught as the opposition pair.

Unresolved points persisting:
* Whether Arabesque III retains II opposition with supporting-side forward arm, or switches to effacée with forward arm on working-leg side.
* Whether Arabesque IV is a croisée opposition like II with a clear forward arm opposite leg, or a closed/effacée inclined variant where the clear forward extension is lost/rounded.
* The precise meaning of “arm extended in front” – textbook croisée label vs studio practice of a distinct forward extension at shoulder height.
* Nomenclature drift between ouvert/effacée vs croisée labeling across teachers/sources.

Current belief state: II is secure. The weight of public argument in round 2 remains with E. Second and fourth, with a coherent, repeated croisée II/IV reading and I/III ouvert/effacée reading. The B minority raises a credible practical point about the clarity of forward extension in IV and preservation of opposition in III. I am leaning toward E. Second and fourth as the most coherent Vaganova croisée pair, while retaining uncertainty about the exact port de bras definition of III and the exact studio treatment of IV’s forward extension.

The core undisputed premise remains that Arabesque II is the classic Vaganova croisée opposition/croisée arabesque: body in profile on the supporting leg, working leg en arabesque behind, supporting-side arm brought forward at shoulder height and working-side arm taken back, so the forward arm is on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg.

* II = croisée opposition as above.
* IV = inclined croisée / cambré variant of II, same opposition logic retained: forward arm supporting side, back arm working side, forward arm opposite lifted leg; difference is deeper épaulement/inclination and lower carriage.

* II = classic croisée opposition as above.
* III = lower/softened/open version of II, torso more opened/cambré, carriage lower/rounded, but arm logic preserved: supporting-side arm still projected forward in front of torso and working-side arm still back/up along line of leg, so forward arm remains opposite lifted leg. II and III are routinely taught as a paired opposition family, III being the cambré/softened II.

The phrase “arm extended in front” is interpreted differently: E treats it as a clear front-back ligne with one arm distinctly in front on supporting side; B treats any forward carriage of supporting-side arm, even low/rounded, as qualifying.

My current best belief remains E. Second and fourth are the Vaganova croisée arabesques with the dancer’s arm extended in front on the opposite side to the lifted leg. I and III are the ouvert/effacée pair where that clear opposite-side forward projection is absent or reversed. reflection_text.7:
The question is which Vaganova arabesques have the supporting-side arm carried extended in front, i.e. on the opposite side to the lifted/working leg behind.

Core agreement:
* Arabesque II is undisputed classic croisée/contraposed opposition: body in profile on supporting leg, working leg en arabesque derrière, supporting-side arm brought forward at shoulder height in front of torso, working-side arm taken back in line with leg. Forward arm is opposite the lifted leg.
* Arabesque I is ouvert/en face/effacée: arms essentially in wide second/open, frontal/symmetrical, no clear single forward cross on supporting side; any forward bias is on working-leg side.

Split is I/III vs IV, and III vs IV.

E camp – II and IV are the croisée pair, I and III are ouvert/effacée/open.
* Arabesque III = effacée/open: arms brought together in front in Vaganova 3rd/effacée port de bras. Forward/leading arm is on the working/lifted side, i.e. forward carriage is on same side as lifted leg; classic front-back opposition is lost/reversed.
* Arabesque IV = croisée inclinée/cambré variant of II. Same arm logic as II: forward arm remains supporting-side, back arm working-side. Difference is deeper cambré/inclination and lower carriage, not reversal of opposition.
Therefore forward-arm-opposite-leg arabesques are II and IV. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7 reiterate this in round 2, stressing I & III as ouvert/effacée and II & IV as croisée.

B camp – II and III are the opposition pair, I and IV break the pattern.
* Arabesque III keeps II opposition logic, just lower/softened/cambré. Supporting-side arm is still projected forward in front of torso, working-side arm back/up. Forward arm remains opposite lifted leg; teachers routinely pair II+III as opposition arabesques.
* Arabesque IV is closed/inclined/effacée with port de bras IV: arms move toward rounded second/fourth, brought closer to body and more to side, clear supporting-side forward extension at shoulder height is lost/ softened. In studio practice forward projection is no longer reliably on opposite side.
Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9 argue this in round 2, emphasizing the wording “arm extended in front” as stricter than generic opposition.

Remaining uncertainty:
* Numbering/convention variability across studios.
* Precise description of Arabesque III arm placement: E camp says forward arm shifts to working-leg side in effacée 3rd port de bras; B camp says forward arm stays supporting-side but lower/rounded.
* Whether Arabesque IV retains a clear “extended in front” arm or is a lower, rounded, closed carriage where the clear front extension is lost.

I remain leaning to E. Second and fourth as the intended answer, with the croisée vs ouvert/effacée distinction driving it: II and IV are the Vaganova croisée arabesques with forward arm on supporting/opposite side to lifted leg, I and III are the ouvert/effacée forms where forward emphasis is on working-leg side or lost. reflection_text.15:
The question is about Vaganova arabesque port de bras and which arabesques have a clear single arm extended in front on the supporting side, i.e. on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg.

Core taxonomy still in play:

* Arabesque II – croisée / contraposed / opposition. Body en profil on supporting leg, working leg en arabesque derrière. Port de bras is long front-back line: supporting-side arm brought forward at shoulder height in front of torso, working-side arm taken back in line with leg. Forward arm is on opposite side to lifted leg. Un disputed.
* Arabesque III – effacée / open. Described by the E majority as effacée port de bras III: arms brought more together in front of body, forward-prominent/leading arm on working-leg side, i.e. forward arm is on same side as lifted leg or opposition is lost/reversed. Described by B minority as lower/softened continuation of II: supporting-side arm still projected forward opposite lifted leg, working-side arm back, just lower/rounded/cambré.
* Arabesque IV – croisée inclinée / cambré. Described by E majority as variant of II: torso more inclined/cambré but arm logic retained, forward arm remains supporting-side arm in front of torso, back arm remains working-leg side. Forward arm again opposite lifted leg; difference is degree of épaulement/inclination, not reversal of opposition. Described by B minority as closed/inclined/effacée with arms more rounded/second/fourth, forward projection lost or no longer a clean arm extended in front on supporting side.

Round 2 public distribution: strong E majority, Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7 all arguing E. Second and fourth, II and IV are the croisée opposition pair with front-arm-opposite/back-arm-same contraposition, I and III are ouvert/effacée with forward emphasis on working-leg side or lost. B minority, Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9, arguing B. Second and third, II is classic opposition and III retains the same opposition principle with lower/softened/cambré carriage, forward arm still supporting-side opposite lifted leg; IV is the closed/rounded/effacée variant where clear forward extension on supporting side is lost.

Key arguments for E: Vaganova codification names croisée arabesques II and IV; III is effacée port de bras with arms together in front, leading arm on working side; I and III form the ouvert/effacée pair. Textbook épaulement descriptions cite II/IV as croisée.

Key arguments for B: studio practice pairs II and III as opposition pair, II high classical, III lower cambré continuation; IV loses clear front extension because torso deeply cambré and arms rounded/closed fourth-type, forward projection not cleanly “extended in front”. Question wording “arm extended in front” is stricter than generic opposition.

Unresolved: exact studio teaching variance for Arabesque III vs IV and how strictly “arm extended in front” is interpreted – whether III’s lower/rounded port de bras III still counts as an arm “extended in front” on the opposite side, and whether IV’s deeper cambré still presents a cleanly forward-projected supporting-side arm. Naming inconsistencies persist between colleagues who swap I/III vs II/IV labels.

My current understanding remains that the textbook Vaganova codification names the croisée opposition as Arabesque II and Arabesque IV, with the forward arm on the supporting/opposite side to the lifted leg, while Arabesque I is ouvert and Arabesque III is effacée/open with forward prominence on the working side. * Arabesque II = croisée/opposition. Body in profile on supporting leg, working leg behind. Port de bras long front-back: supporting-side arm forward at shoulder height, working-side arm back. Forward arm opposite lifted leg.

reflection_text.6:
Vaganova arabesque arm opposition remains the core. Arabesque II is undisputed across all accounts: body en profil / croisée, working leg derrière, supporting-side arm carried forward in front of torso, working-side arm carried back. Forward arm is on the opposite side to the lifted leg.

The entire dispute is III vs IV for the second position with an arm extended in front on the opposite side.

E. Second and fourth camp, now dominant in round 2, maps Vaganova as two croisée, two ouvert/effacée:
* I = ouvert/en face, arms wide second/open, no clear forward cross, any forward bias on working side.
* III = effacée/open, arms brought together in front in port de bras III/effacée, leading/forward arm is on working/lifted side, torso opened effacée to leg. Non-croisée. Forward arm same side as leg.
* II = croisée/opposition, classic front-back opposition, forward arm supporting side = opposite lifted leg.
* IV = croisée inclinée/cambré, same croisée arm logic as II but with deeper cambré/inclination and lower back arm. Forward arm remains supporting-side = opposite lifted leg.

This gives croisée pair II & IV with opposite-side forward arm, ouvert/effacée pair I & III with forward arm on same side or no clear forward cross. Supporting evidence repeatedly cited is croisée vs effacée terminology and “two croisés, two effacés” consistency, with III described as effacée with forward arm on working side and IV described as inclined opposition.

B. Second and third camp argues:
* II = classic croisée opposition, forward arm opposite lifted leg.
* III = lower/softened/open variant of II, torso more opened/cambré, arm carriage lower/rounded but arm logic preserved: supporting-side arm still projected forward, working-side arm back. Forward arm remains opposite lifted leg. Teachers routinely pair II and III as the opposition arabesques.
* I = ouvert second, no clear forward opposite arm.
* IV = closed/effacée/rounded fourth port de bras, arms brought more together/forward, clear supporting-side forward projection lost or shifted toward working side, or not a crisp “extended in front”.

Key B evidence is pedagogical pairing of II & III as opposition, III retaining same supporting-side forward arm albeit softer/lower, and IV taught as closed/rounded with lost opposition. B also stresses the wording “arm extended in front” is stricter than generic opposition; IV’s deeply cambré, lowered/rounded carriage is not a clear extension in front.

The definition of “extended in front” — crisp shoulder-height projection vs softer rounded/inclined projection — drives the III vs IV disagreement.

Current working weight remains with E Second and fourth due to majority weight and systematic croisée/effacée mapping, though I retain uncertainty on whether III’s effacée description with forward arm on working side is a stable textbook fact or a conflation of port de bras numbering, and whether IV’s inclined cambré still satisfies “arm extended in front”.
reflection_text.11:
The question is Vaganova arabesque derrière with specific port de bras/épaulement: an arm clearly extended in front on the supporting side, i.e. opposite the lifted leg.

Core stable point: Arabesque II is undisputed classic croisée/opposition. Body en profil on the supporting leg, working leg en arabesque derrière, supporting-side arm brought forward at shoulder height in front of the torso and working-side arm taken back in line with the leg. Forward arm is on the opposite side to the lifted leg.

The split is III vs IV.

E majority in round 2 – Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7 – describe:
* Arabesque I ouvert/en face/effacée. Arms essentially wide second/open, symmetrical/frontal, no clear single forward arm on supporting side; any forward bias is on working/lifted side.
* Arabesque III effacée/open. Arms brought together in front in Vaganova 3rd/effacée port de bras. Leading/forward arm is on the working/lifted side, torso opened effacée to that leg. Forward arm is on same side as lifted leg, opposition reversed/lost. I and III are the ouvert/effacée pair.
* Arabesque II croisée/opposition as above.
* Arabesque IV croisée inclinée/cambré. Same croisée opposition logic as II, torso deeper cambré/inclined, forward arm remains supporting-side arm in front, back arm on working-leg side. Forward arm again opposite lifted leg. II/IV are the croisée pair.

Hence the forward-on-opposite-side pattern belongs to the croisée pair II and IV.

B minority – Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9 – argue:
* Arabesque II undisputed classic opposition with forward arm opposite lifted leg.
* Arabesque III retains that same opposition principle, just lower/softer/more cambré. Supporting-side arm still projected forward opposite leg; change is height/shaping, not reversal. II and III are routinely paired as opposition arabesques.
* Arabesque I ouvert with no forward opposition.
* Arabesque IV is closed/rounded/effacée, port de bras moves toward rounded second/4th, forward supporting-side projection lost or not clearly extended in front.

Disagreement therefore centres on classification of III vs IV: is III the effacée same-side forward arm with IV the inclined opposition, or is III the softened opposition with IV the closed effacée.

Round 2 shows convergence toward E: several colleagues who previously argued A/C have shifted to E, and the E count is now ~12 vs B ~6. The cross-referenced Vaganova description that remains most stable in the discussion is croisée arabesques are II and IV and ouvert/effacée are I and III.

Residual uncertainty remains naming variability across teaching vocabularies – some teachers label the opposition pair as II/III and treat IV as effacée – which is source of persistent B minority. For Vaganova as codified in this deliberation the best current understanding remains E. Second and fourth, with II as high classic croisée opposition and IV as its inclined cambré variant, while I and III are ouvert/effacée forms where the clear opposite-side forward arm is lost or reversed.

III retains same opposition principle but with lower/more cambré torso and softer/rounded arm carriage; supporting-side arm is still projected forward in front of torso opposite lifted leg. * Vaganova numbering is defined by port de bras/épaulement, not leg alone.

3.text:
**E. Second and fourth**

The four Vaganova arabesques derrière share the same leg attitude and are distinguished by épaulement / port de bras.

* Arabesque I – ouvert / en face. Arms stay essentially in a wide second / open line about the frontal plane, more or less symmetrical. There is no clear single arm projected forward on the supporting side; any forward bias is on the working / lifted side.

* Arabesque III – effacée / open. Arms are brought together in front of the torso in the Vaganova 3rd / effacée port de bras. The torso is opened effacée to the working leg and the leading / forward arm is on the working / lifted side. The forward prominence is therefore on the same side as the lifted leg and the classic front-back opposition is lost / reversed. I and III are the ouvert/effacée pair.

The croisée / opposition pair is II and IV.

* Arabesque II – croisée classic opposition. Body en profil on the supporting leg, working leg en arabesque derrière. Port de bras is a long front-back line: the supporting-side arm is brought forward at shoulder height in front of the torso and the working-side arm is taken back in line with the leg. The forward arm is therefore on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg.

* Arabesque IV – croisée inclinée / cambré. The same opposition principle as II is retained with a deeper cambré / inclination of the torso and a lower carriage of the back arm. The supporting-side arm remains carried forward in front of the torso and the working-side arm remains on the working-leg side. The forward arm is again the supporting-side arm, i.e. on the opposite side to the lifted working leg. II is the higher classical version, IV is the inclined / deeper version of the same croisée opposition.

It is therefore the two croisée arabesques, II and IV, that give the characteristic Vaganova front-arm-opposite / back-arm-same contraposition with a dancer’s arm extended in front on the opposite side to the lifted leg. I and III are the ouvert / effacée forms where that clear opposite-side forward projection is lost or reversed.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’ve been following the croisée vs ouvert/effacée framing and it’s been really helpful for clarifying I and III. II is clearly the textbook croisée opposition: body en profil on the supporting leg, working leg en arabesque derrière, supporting-side arm brought forward at shoulder height in front of the torso and working-side arm taken back in line with the leg. The forward arm is unambiguously on the opposite side to the lifted leg.

Where I’m getting stuck on the II/IV pairing is the specific wording of the question: an arm *extended in front* on the opposite side to the lifted leg.

IV is described as the croisée inclinée / cambré variant of II, and the opposition logic is the same in principle. In practice in Vaganova studio work the port de bras of IV is not the same clean extension in front you get in II. The torso is deeply cambré/inclined, the épaulement closes, and the arms move toward a more rounded, closed second/fourth-type carriage. The supporting-side arm is dropped, softened and brought closer to the body and more to the side rather than being projected forward at shoulder height in front of the torso. The crisp front-back line of II is lost. That is why IV is often taught as the closed/inclined, more effacée/rounded variant where the clear forward extension is no longer reliable.

III, by contrast, does keep that forward-on-the-supporting-side projection, just in a lower, softer shape. It is taught as the lower/cambré development of II. The torso opens a little more, the carriage is more cambré and the port de bras is lower and more rounded than in II, but the arm logic is preserved: the arm on the standing/supporting side is still the one projected forward in front of the torso and the arm on the working-leg side is still carried back/up along the line of the leg. The forward arm remains the supporting-side arm, i.e. opposite the lifted leg, with a softer, more inclined line than II.

I is the ouvert/en face form with the arms essentially in a wide second/open line, no clear single arm projected forward on the supporting side.

So on the criterion of an arm that is actually extended in front of the torso on the supporting side, opposite the lifted leg, the two positions that reliably give that clear forward projection in teaching practice are II and III. II is the high classical opposition and III is the same opposition with a deeper cambré and lower arm placement. IV loses the clear forward extension in front.

That puts me at B. Second and third.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: B. Second and third

I think we are getting very close and the disagreement is really about how strictly we read "arm extended in front" and how IV is taught in practice.

Arabesque II is undisputed for everyone. Body en profil on the supporting leg, working leg en arabesque derrière, port de bras in true front-back opposition: the supporting-side arm is brought forward at shoulder height in front of the torso and the working-side arm is taken back in line with the leg. The forward arm is on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg. That is the classic Vaganova croisée opposition.

Arabesque III keeps that same arm logic in class. It is the lower / more cambré, softer development of II. The torso opens a little more, the épaulement is deeper and the carriage is lower, the port de bras is more rounded and the arms sit a little closer to the body, but the opposition is preserved: the arm belonging to the standing/supporting side is still the one projected forward in front of the torso and the arm belonging to the working side is still carried back/up along the line of the leg. The forward arm remains the supporting-side arm, i.e. on the opposite side to the lifted leg, just with a softer, more inclined shaping than in II. That is why II and III are routinely paired in the syllabus as the opposition arabesques, II being the high classical opposition and III being the same opposition with a deeper cambré and lower arm placement.

Arabesque I is the ouvert / en face form. The arms stay essentially in a wide second / open line, essentially symmetrical about the frontal plane, with no clear single arm projected forward on the supporting side.

Arabesque IV is where the clear "arm extended in front" criterion starts to break down in studio practice. IV is the closed / inclined / effacée variant. The torso is deeply cambré and inclined, the épaulement closes, and the port de bras moves toward a more rounded second / fourth attitude, arms brought more together and rounded in front of the body rather than in a clean front-back line. The crisp supporting-side forward extension you have in II and, in a lower shape, in III is softened and the arm is no longer reliably projected extended in front of the torso on the supporting side in the same way; the line is taught as more rounded and to the side.

reflection_text.4:

The dispute remains tightly concentrated on the partner to II: II + IV vs II + III.

E. Second and fourth camp, still plurality in round 3:
* Arabesque I = ouvert/en face/effacée, arms in wide second/open, essentially symmetrical/frontal, no clear forward cross on supporting side; any forward bias is on working-leg side.

* Arabesque IV = croisée inclinée/cambré, same opposition principle as II retained with deeper cambré/inclination; forward arm remains supporting-side in front of torso, back arm on working-leg side. II/IV are the Vaganova croisée pair. Difference between II and IV is degree of épaulement/inclination, not reversal of opposition.

B. Second and third camp, persistent minority:
* Arabesque I = ouvert/en face, arms in low second/open, no clear forward opposition.
* Arabesque IV = closed/rounded second/4th/effacée inclined variant; torso more cambré, arms move toward rounded second/fourth, forward projection is softened/lost, no longer a clear arm extended in front on supporting side opposite leg.
* Arabesque II = classic opposition, forward arm opposite lifted leg.
* Arabesque III = lower/softened cambré development of II, torso more opened/lower/cambré but arm logic preserved: supporting-side arm still forward in front of torso, working-side arm back; forward arm remains opposite lifted leg. Unresolved points persisting:

* Whether Arabesque IV is a croisée opposition like II with a clear forward arm opposite leg, or a closed/effacée inclined variant where the clear forward extension is lost/rounded.

reflection_text.1:
The core definitional feature remains: supporting-side arm forward in front of torso = forward arm on opposite side to lifted leg, working-side arm back in line with leg.

II is undisputed across all colleagues as the classic Vaganova croisée/opposition arabesque with body en profil on supporting leg, working leg derrière, supporting-side arm forward at shoulder height in front of torso, working-side arm back. Forward arm is opposite lifted leg.

Dispute is mapping of III and IV.

E camp – Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7 in Round 3 – holds Vaganova croisée/opposition pair is II and IV, ouvert/effacée pair is I and III. 
* I = ouvert/en face, arms wide second/open, frontal/symmetrical, no clear supporting-side forward projection.
* III = effacée/open, port de bras III/effacée, arms brought together in front of torso, torso opened effacée to working leg, leading/forward arm on working/lifted side, forward prominence same side as lifted leg. Classic front-back opposition lost/reversed.
* II = croisée classic opposition, supporting-side arm forward opposite lifted leg.
* IV = croisée inclinée/cambré, same opposition principle retained with deeper cambré/inclination/deeper épaulement, supporting-side arm remains carried forward in front of torso, working-side arm back. IV is inclined/deeper version of II, not a reversal.

B camp – Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9 in Round 3 – holds opposition pair is II and III, IV loses clear forward extension.
* II = undisputed opposite-side forward arm.
* III = lower/more cambré/softer development of II, torso opens more, port de bras lower/rounded but arm logic preserved: standing/supporting-side arm still projected forward in front of torso, working-side arm back/up. Forward arm remains supporting-side/opposite lifted leg, just lower/inclined.
* I = ouvert/en face, arms wide second, no clear forward opposition.
* IV = closed/inclined/effacée variant where crisp supporting-side forward projection is softened/lost; port de bras moves toward rounded second/4th, arms brought more together in front/side, forward placement no longer reliably opposite/extended in front. Hence criterion “arm extended in front” fails for IV.

Round 3 public split is E. Second and fourth – 12 colleagues, B. Second and third – 6 colleagues. Majority moved toward E in Round 2 and held in Round 3, strengthening II/IV croisée pairing.

Key preserved errors/confusions: terminology mixing between ouvert/effacée vs croisée and port de bras I-III vs arabesque I-IV; disagreement whether Vaganova III is effacée same-side-forward with port de bras III, or lower opposition retaining opposite-side forward arm; disagreement whether IV is inclined croisée retaining opposition or closed/rounded effacée with forward projection lost.

Unresolved: need authoritative textual source to settle whether canonical Vaganova III retains II opposition with lower carriage or is the effacée same-side-forward arabesque, and whether IV is inclined croisée opposition or closed effacée variant.

reflection_text.15:
The question is which Vaganova arabesques keep a clear single arm projected extended in front on the supporting side, i.e. opposite the lifted leg.

Core taxonomy in play:
* Arabesque I – ouvert/en face. Arms essentially wide second/open, essentially frontal/symmetrical; any forward bias is on working/lifted side. No clear forward-opposite arm.
* Arabesque II – croisée / contraposed opposition. Body en profil on supporting leg, working leg derrière. Port de bras is long front-back line: supporting-side arm brought forward at shoulder height in front of torso, working-side arm back in line with leg. Forward arm is unambiguously opposite lifted leg. Un disputed.
* Arabesque III – effacée/open. E majority: Vaganova effacée/3rd port de bras, arms brought together in front of torso, leading/forward arm on working/lifted side, forward prominence same side as lifted leg, classic front-back opposition lost/reversed. I and III are the ouvert/effacée pair.
  B minority: III is lower/softened/cambré continuation of II. Torso opens more, carriage lower, port de bras more rounded, but arm logic preserved: supporting-side arm still projected forward in front of torso, working-side arm back. Forward arm remains opposite lifted leg, just lower/rounded. II and III routinely paired in class as opposition pair, II high classical, III lower cambré.
* Arabesque IV – croisée inclinée/cambré. E majority: variant of II. Deeper cambré/inclination and deeper épaulement, but opposition principle retained: supporting-side arm remains carried forward in front of torso, working-side arm back. Forward arm again opposite lifted leg; difference is degree of inclination, not reversal.
  B minority: IV loses the clean “arm extended in front” criterion. IV is taught as closed/inclined/effacée with torso deeply cambré, épaulement closes, port de bras moves toward rounded second/fourth, arms brought more together/rounded in front of body rather than clean front-back line. The crisp supporting-side forward extension is softened/lost.

Second and fourth, II and IV are croisée opposition pair with front-arm-opposite/back-arm-same contraposition, I and III are ouvert/effacée with forward emphasis on working-leg side or lost. B minority Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9 argue B. Unresolved: exact studio teaching variance for Arabesque III vs IV and how strictly “arm extended in front” is interpreted – whether III’s lower/rounded port de bras III still counts as an arm “extended in front” on the opposite side, and whether IV’s deeper cambré still presents a cleanly forward-projected supporting-side arm. * Arabesque I is ouvert/en face/effacée: arms essentially in wide second/open, frontal/symmetrical, no clear single forward cross on supporting side; any forward bias is on working-leg side.

Split is I/III vs IV, and III vs IV.

E camp – II and IV are the croisée pair, I and III are ouvert/effacée/open.
* Arabesque III = effacée/open: arms brought together in front in Vaganova 3rd/effacée port de bras. Forward/leading arm is on working/lifted side, i.e. forward carriage is on same side as lifted leg; classic front-back opposition is lost/reversed.
* Arabesque IV = croisée inclinée/cambré variant of II. Same arm logic as II: forward arm remains supporting-side, back arm working-side. Difference is deeper cambré/inclination and lower carriage, not reversal of opposition.

* Arabesque IV is closed/inclined/effacée with port de bras IV: arms move toward rounded second/fourth, brought closer to body and more to side, clear supporting-side forward extension at shoulder height is lost/softened. In studio practice forward projection is no longer reliably on opposite side.

Second and fourth as the intended textbook distinction: II and IV are Vaganova croisée arabesques with forward arm on supporting/opposite side to lifted leg, I and III are ouvert/effacée forms where forward emphasis is on working-leg side or lost. reflection_text.11:
The leg attitude is the same in all four Vaganova arabesques derrière; the four are distinguished by épaulement / port de bras.

Core stable point remains undisputed: Arabesque II is classic croisée opposition. Body en profil on the supporting leg, working leg en arabesque derrière, supporting-side arm brought forward at shoulder height in front of the torso and working-side arm taken back in line with the leg. Forward arm is unambiguously on the opposite side to the lifted leg.

The persistent split is III vs IV.

E majority, now ~12 of 18 in round 3, Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7, holds the codified croisée pair = II and IV and ouvert/effacée pair = I and III.

* Arabesque I – ouvert/en face. Arms essentially wide second/open, symmetrical/frontal, no clear single arm projected forward on the supporting side; any forward bias is on the working-leg side.
* Arabesque III – effacée/open. Arms brought together in front in Vaganova 3rd/effacée port de bras. Body opened effacée to the working leg and the leading/forward arm is on the working/lifted side, i.e. forward prominence on the same side as the lifted leg. Classic front-back croisée opposition is lost/reversed.
* Arabesque II – croisée classic opposition as above.
* Arabesque IV – croisée inclinée/cambré. Same opposition principle as II retained with deeper cambré/inclination and deeper épaulement. Supporting-side arm remains carried forward in front of the torso, working-side arm back on working-leg side. Forward arm again opposite lifted leg; IV is the inclined/deeper version of the same croisée opposition.

Thus the two positions with an arm extended in front on the supporting side, opposite the lifted leg, are II and IV.

B minority, Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9, argues II is undisputed and III retains the same opposition logic, just lower/softer/more cambré. Supporting-side arm is still projected forward opposite the leg, working-side arm back. II and III are routinely paired as the opposition arabesques, II high classical, III lower cambré continuation. Arabesque IV is described in studio practice as the closed/rounded/effacée variant: torso deeply cambré, épaulement closes, port de bras moves toward a rounded second/4th, arms brought more together in front and to the side, crisp supporting-side forward extension softened/lost. Arabesque I is ouvert/en face with no clear forward opposition.

Disagreement therefore remains about naming variability: is III the effacée same-side forward arm with IV the inclined opposition, or is III the softened opposition with IV the closed effacée? The wording “arm extended in front” is the source of the B argument that IV loses a distinct extended-in-front projection while III keeps it in a lower shape.

Evidence of convergence: colleagues who previously argued A/C, e.g. 17,18, have now shifted to E. The cross-referenced Vaganova description that remains most stable in the discussion is croisée = II/IV and ouvert/effacée = I/III.

Unresolved: precise studio teaching of IV port de bras – clear forward supporting-side extension vs rounded closed carriage – and whether III’s effacée port de bras should be read as forward arm on the working side or as a lower opposition with forward arm still on the supporting side. Current best understanding with the codified croisée/ouvert framing remains E, second and fourth, with II as high classic croisée opposition and IV as its inclined cambré variant, while I and III are the ouvert/effacée forms where the clear opposite-side forward projection is lost or reversed.

**E. Second and fourth**

The leg is en arabesque derrière in all four Vaganova arabesques. The four positions are distinguished by épaulement / port de bras, not by the leg line.

* Arabesque I – ouvert / en face. Arms essentially in a wide second / open line about the frontal plane. The carriage is essentially symmetrical/frontal and any forward bias is on the working / lifted side. There is no single clear arm projected forward on the supporting side.

* Arabesque III – effacée / open. The arms are brought together in front of the torso in the Vaganova effacée / 3rd port de bras. The torso is opened effacée to the working leg and the leading / forward arm is on the working / lifted side, i.e. the forward prominence is on the same side as the lifted leg. The classic front-back croisée opposition is lost / reversed. I and III are the ouvert/effacée pair.

The croisée / opposition pair is II and IV.

* Arabesque II – croisée / classic opposition. Body en profil on the supporting leg, working leg en arabesque derrière. Port de bras is a long front-back line: the supporting-side arm is brought forward at shoulder height in front of the torso and the working-side arm is taken back in line with the leg. The forward arm is therefore on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg.

* Arabesque IV – croisée inclinée / cambré. The same opposition principle as II is retained with a deeper cambré / inclination of the torso and a deeper épaulement. The supporting-side arm remains carried forward in front of the torso and the working-side arm remains carried back in line with the leg. The forward arm is again the supporting-side arm, i.e. on the opposite side to the lifted working leg; IV is the inclined / deeper version of the same croisée opposition, II being the higher classical version.

It is therefore the two croisée arabesques, II and IV, that give the characteristic Vaganova front-arm-opposite / back-arm-same contraposition with a dancer’s arm extended in front on the supporting side, i.e. on the opposite side to the lifted leg. I and III are the ouvert / effacée forms where that clear opposite-side forward projection is lost or reversed.

**B. Second and third**

* Arabesque II is undisputed classic croisée opposition: supporting-side arm forward opposite lifted leg, working-side arm back.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is which Vaganova arabesques derrière have a dancer’s arm actually extended in front of the torso on the supporting side, i.e. on the opposite side to the lifted/working leg behind.

Core agreement:
* Arabesque II is undisputed classic croisée/contraposed opposition: body en profil on supporting leg, working leg en arabesque derrière, supporting-side arm brought forward at shoulder height in front of torso, working-side arm taken back in line with leg. Forward arm is opposite the lifted leg.
* Arabesque I is ouvert/en face/effacée: arms essentially in wide second/open, frontal/symmetrical, no clear single forward cross on supporting side; any forward bias is on working-leg side.

Split is II+IV vs II+III, and specifically how III and IV are taught.

E camp – II and IV are the croisée pair, I and III are ouvert/effacée/open.
* Arabesque III = effacée/open with Vaganova 3rd/effacée port de bras. Arms brought together in front of torso, torso opened effacée to working leg. Leading/forward arm is on working/lifted side, forward prominence is on same side as lifted leg; classic front-back opposition is lost/reversed.
* Arabesque IV = croisée inclinée/cambré variant of II. Same arm logic as II: forward arm remains supporting-side, back arm working-side. Difference is deeper cambré/inclination and lower carriage, not reversal of opposition.
Therefore forward-arm-opposite-leg arabesques are II and IV. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7 in round 4 reiterate this with explicit croisée vs ouvert/effacée framing.

* Arabesque IV is closed/inclined/effacée with port de bras IV: arms move toward rounded second/fourth, brought closer to body and more to side, clear supporting-side forward extension at shoulder height is lost/softened. In studio practice forward projection is no longer reliably on opposite side.

I remain leaning to E. Second and fourth as the intended textbook distinction: II and IV are Vaganova croisée arabesques with forward arm on supporting/opposite side to lifted leg, I and III are ouvert/effacée forms where forward emphasis is on working-leg side or lost. * Arabesque I – ouvert/en face. Arms essentially wide second/open, frontal/symmetrical. No clear single forward opposite-side arm; any forward bias is on the working/lifted side.
* Arabesque II – croisée / classic opposition. Body en profil on supporting leg, working leg derrière. * Arabesque III – dispute. E majority: effacée/open. reflection_text.15:
The question is which Vaganova arabesques derrière keep a single arm projected/cleanly extended in front of the torso on the supporting side, i.e. the arm on the opposite side of the body to the lifted working leg.

Core taxonomy in play:
* Arabesque I – ouvert/en face. Arms essentially wide second/open, frontal/symmetrical. No clear single forward opposite-side arm; any forward bias is on the working/lifted side.
* Arabesque II – croisée / classic opposition. Body en profil on supporting leg, working leg derrière. Port de bras is long front-back line: supporting-side arm brought forward at shoulder height in front of torso, working-side arm back in line with leg. Forward arm unambiguously opposite lifted leg. Undisputed.
* Arabesque III – dispute. E majority: effacée/open. Vaganova effacée/3rd port de bras, arms brought together in front of torso, torso opened effacée to working leg, leading/forward arm on working/lifted side. Forward prominence is same side as lifted leg; classic front-back croisée opposition lost/reversed. I and III form ouvert/effacée pair.
  B minority: III is lower/softened/cambré continuation of II. Torso opened more, carriage lower, port de bras more rounded, but arm logic preserved: supporting-side arm still projected forward in front of torso, working-side arm back. Forward arm remains opposite lifted leg, just lower/rounded. II and III routinely paired in class as opposition pair, II high classical, III lower cambré.
* Arabesque IV – dispute. E majority: croisée inclinée/cambré. Variant of II. Deeper cambré/inclination and deeper épaulement, but opposition principle retained: supporting-side arm remains carried forward in front of torso, working-side arm back. Forward arm again opposite lifted leg; difference is degree of inclination, not reversal. II/IV are the croisée pair.
  B minority: IV loses the clean “arm extended in front” criterion. IV is taught as closed/inclined/effacée with torso deeply cambré, épaulement closes, port de bras moves toward rounded second/fourth, arms brought more together/rounded in front of body rather than clean front-back line. The crisp supporting-side forward extension is softened/lost.

Round 4 public distribution mirrors round 3. E. Second and fourth holds a strong majority: Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7 argue II and IV are the croisée opposition pair with front-arm-opposite/back-arm-same contraposition, I and III are ouvert/effacée with forward emphasis on working-leg side or lost.
B. Second and third minority: Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9 argue II is classic opposition and III retains same opposition principle with lower/softened/cambré carriage, forward arm still supporting-side opposite lifted leg; IV is closed/rounded/effacée variant where clear forward extension on supporting side is lost. The key B move is reading the question literally as “arm extended in front” – stricter than generic opposition – and claiming III still shows a distinct forward projection on the supporting side while IV does not.

Key arguments for E: Vaganova codification names croisée arabesques II and IV; textbooks describe épaulement II/IV as croisée, III as effacée port de bras with arms together in front and leading arm on working side; I and III form ouvert/effacée pair.
Key arguments for B: studio practice pairs II and III as opposition pair, II high classical, III lower cambré continuation; IV loses clear front extension because torso deeply cambré and arms rounded/closed fourth-type, forward projection not cleanly “extended in front”. Question wording is stricter than generic opposition.

Notable shifts in round 4: several colleagues who previously argued A/C positions have moved to E second and fourth, reinforcing the E majority. The split remains between textbook codification naming II/IV as croisée vs studio teaching emphasis on II/III as opposition pair and on the literal “extended in front” placement.

Unresolved: exact studio teaching variance for Arabesque III vs IV and how strictly “arm extended in front” is interpreted – whether III’s lower/rounded port de bras III still counts as an arm “extended in front” on the opposite side, and whether IV’s deeper cambré still presents a cleanly forward-projected supporting-side arm. Naming inconsistencies between colleagues who swap I/III vs II/IV labels persist.

Current working understanding remains that textbook Vaganova codification names the croisée opposition as Arabesque II and Arabesque IV with forward arm on supporting/opposite side to lifted leg, while Arabesque I is ouvert and Arabesque III is effacée/open with forward prominence on working side. That aligns with E. Second and fourth, even though the B camp maintains III keeps opposition and IV loses the clear forward extension. Majority weight in rounds 2-4 is E.
reflection_text.12:
The core undisputed premise persists across rounds: Vaganova Arabesque II is the classic croisée opposition – body en profil on the supporting leg, working leg en arabesque derrière, long front-back port de bras with the supporting-side arm brought forward at shoulder height in front of the torso and the working-side arm taken back in line with the leg. The forward arm is unambiguously on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg.

The dispute is which other arabesque shares that forward-opposite arm line, and how the wording “arm extended in front” is interpreted.

E camp – Second and fourth, Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7, ~12 votes in round 4:
* I = ouvert/en face, arms wide second/open, essentially symmetrical/frontal, no clear single forward projection on supporting side; any forward bias is on working-leg side.
* III = effacée/open, Vaganova effacée/3rd port de bras, arms brought together in front, torso opened effacée to working leg, leading/forward arm is on working/lifted side, i.e. forward prominence is on same side as lifted leg. Classic front-back croisée opposition is lost/reversed. I and III are the ouvert/effacée pair.
* II = croisée classic opposition as above.
* IV = croisée inclinée/cambré, same opposition principle retained with deeper cambré/inclination and deeper épaulement. Supporting-side arm remains carried forward in front of torso, working-side arm remains back on working-leg side. Forward arm again on opposite side to lifted leg. II is higher classical version, IV is inclined/deeper version of same croisée opposition.

Hence E claims the two croisée arabesques II and IV give the characteristic front-arm-opposite/back-arm-same contraposition with an arm extended in front on supporting side opposite lifted leg.

B camp – Second and third, Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9, ~6 votes in round 4:
* II undisputed as classic croisée opposition.
* III keeps same opposition logic, taught as lower/more cambré/softened development of II. Torso opens more, épaulement deeper, carriage lower/rounded, port de bras more rounded and closer to body, but arm logic preserved: arm on standing/supporting side still projected forward in front of torso and arm on working side still carried back/up along line of leg. Forward arm remains supporting-side i.e. opposite lifted leg, just with softer/inclined shaping. II and III routinely grouped as opposition family, II high classical, III same opposition with deeper cambré/lower arm placement.
* I = ouvert/en face, arms wide second/open, no clear single arm forward on supporting side.
* IV loses the clear extended-in-front opposition in studio practice. IV is closed/inclined/effacée variant. Torso deeply cambré/inclined, épaulement closes, port de bras moves toward rounded second/fourth attitude, arms brought more together/rounded in front of body and more to side. Crisp supporting-side forward extension of II/III is softened/lost; supporting-side arm dropped/inclined/softened rather than projected extended in front at shoulder height. Forward placement no longer reliably a distinct arm extended in front on opposite side.

B interprets “arm extended in front” literally as a clean forward extension at shoulder height; E treats it as the croisée opposition line even when inclined.

Noticing errors/confusion persists: conflation of port de bras numbering with arabesque numbering; earlier inversions of I/II labels; inconsistent descriptions of III arm placement between “forward arm on working side” vs “supporting side forward”.

My current best belief remains E. Second and fourth are the Vaganova croisée arabesques with the dancer’s arm extended in front on the opposite side to the lifted leg. I and III are the ouvert/effacée pair where that clear opposite-side forward projection is absent or reversed.

Unresolved: whether Vaganova official syllabus/studio practice routinely teaches III with a retained opposite-side forward arm in lower carriage vs III forward arm on working side, and whether IV’s port de bras is truly a clean extended-in-front supporting-side arm or a softened/rounded closed attitude where the “extended in front” criterion fails. A definitive source on Vaganova’s official arabesque IV port de bras description and the exact arm height/shaping in III vs IV is still needed to close the III vs IV ambiguity.
